title: ADRs & Roadmapping
description: A preview of the Planning & Communication toolkit's decision and narrative artifacts.
body: Named artifacts this page previews What a good ADR contains When a decision needs an ADR Roadmaps for two different audiences The business case, stripped to what gets funded ADR conventions that keep the practice alive A worked roadmap example ADR template Four specific templates, beyond the general practice described below. Architecture Decision Record Template, a durable format for hard-to-reverse decisions plus the conventions that keep the practice alive rather than decorative Target-State Narrative Template, a prose-first structure for describing a future operating model to executive audiences, built on the principle that diagrams illustrate clear writing and cannot replace it Capability-Driven Roadmap Method, building multi-year roadmaps rooted in capability gaps rather than technology initiatives, with traceability from strategy to initiative Business Case Template and Narrative, a financial model paired with the narrative structure that makes it defensible to executives and finance reviewers, including a candid options analysis and named benefit owners An Architecture Decision Record exists to answer one question well after the fact: why did we decide this, given what we knew at the time. Most ADR templates fail at exactly that. Section What it should contain Context The situation and constraints as understood at decision time, written before hindsight sets in. This section goes stale fastest and matters most. Decision What was decided, stated in a single clear sentence rather than buried in a paragraph of qualifications. Alternatives considered What else was on the table and why it was rejected. Absence of this section is the most common ADR failure; it's what lets someone later ask "why didn't we just do X" and get a real answer instead of a re-litigation. Consequences What this decision makes harder later. Every architecture decision has a cost; an ADR that lists only benefits is incomplete. Not every choice. Writing one for every minor decision produces the same fatigue problem as over-gating architecture review. When the decision is expensive to reverse, when it affects more than one team, or when you can already predict someone will ask "why did we do it this way" in six months. What counts as expensive to reverse scales with the team, a change that's a quick fix for a three-person startup might be a multi-quarter migration for a five-hundred-engineer org, so weigh it against your own team's capacity rather than a fixed unit of time. Reversible implementation choices scoped entirely within one team, where the cost of writing the record exceeds the cost of just trying something and changing it later if it's wrong. The most common roadmap mistake is one document trying to serve both an engineering audience and a business audience, and serving neither well. Organized by system or capability, includes technical sequencing dependencies, appropriately detailed about implementation approach, timeframes expressed as sprints or quarters. Organized by customer or business outcome, no implementation detail, timeframes expressed as calendar dates tied to business events (a renewal cycle, a fiscal year), directly reusable in the board reporting format described on the Board Reporting page. What separates a business case that gets approved from one that gets deferred indefinitely. A specific, falsifiable claim (this reduces X by Y amount, measured how, by when) tied to a number the approver already tracks, with the cost of not doing it stated as explicitly as the cost of doing it. A business case built entirely around technical merit ("this reduces technical debt") with no connection to a business metric anyone outside engineering tracks. Technical merit is necessary justification, rarely sufficient justification on its own. The template is the easy part. These conventions are what turn a folder of documents into a resource people consult. Numbers are never reused, even for deprecated or superseded ADRs. The number identifies the record; it says nothing about priority. Once accepted, the decision is immutable. Circumstances change, a new ADR supersedes it. Editing the original to reflect current understanding destroys the record. One decision per ADR. A compound ADR is a sign the team is avoiding the harder work of separating decisions. One to two pages. Longer usually means design work leaking in that belongs elsewhere; shorter usually means the alternatives section is missing. Author by role as well as name. "Lead Architect, Payments" carries context that survives staff changes. A compressed real example showing the method end to end: strategic priority through capability gaps through sequenced initiatives. Strategic priority: reduce customer acquisition cost 25 percent within 36 months while maintaining conversion on qualified leads. Capability Gap Initiative Sequence Customer Insight Prospect scoring is rule-based, updated quarterly, limited signal integration Prospect Scoring Modernization Starts first; outputs feed the other two Campaign Management Execution is batch-oriented, attribution manual Campaign Operations Overhaul Starts month 3, overlapping Digital Engagement First response to leads requires human effort, capacity-constrained Early-Stage Engagement Automation Starts month 6, once upstream work is stable A ready-to-use starting point for the format described above: context, decision, alternatives considered, consequences. Markdown for pasting into your own docs system, or a formatted Word doc.

title: Agile and SAFe
body: The four values, and what commonly gets installed instead Why "doing agile" and "being agile" diverge Where SAFe helps Where SAFe becomes its own theater Scaling down deliberately, as well as up Signs agile or SAFe has become theater Each value in the agile manifesto asks for a concrete change in how a team works. Most organizations install a process substitute that satisfies the ritual and skips the substance. Value What it requires What commonly gets installed instead Individuals and interactions over processes and tools Trust, and a team empowered to change its own process A fixed ceremony calendar treated as the definition of agile itself Working software over comprehensive documentation Frequent, real integration and deployment Sprint demos of work that has not been deployed Customer collaboration over contract negotiation Direct, frequent contact between the team and the people using what they build A product owner as the sole interface, recreating the exact handoff agile was meant to remove Responding to change over following a plan A backlog re-prioritized as new information arrives A locked sprint commitment defended against any change, optimizing for predictability over responsiveness The gap that determines whether the ceremonies are earning their keep. The team changes what it does based on what it learns, mid-sprint if warranted, and treats each ceremony as a tool it owns and can modify or drop the moment it stops earning its keep. Standup, retro, planning, and review run on schedule whether or not they produce anything, treated as compliance requirements rather than tools the team controls. The tell: ask when the team last changed its own process because of a retro. Silence answers the question. A real coordination problem exists at scale, and SAFe was built to address it, whatever else gets said about the framework. Coordinating dependencies across many teams building toward a shared release or shared platform, where informal coordination breaks down past a certain team count and someone has to own cross-team sequencing explicitly rather than leaving it to hope. Often cited around 50 to 125 people, five to twelve teams, though the trigger that matters is dependency density between teams, and headcount is only a proxy for it. Ten independent teams with no shared release need none of this; four teams shipping one product together might. The same framework, installed for a coordination problem the organization doesn't have. The framework's ceremonies, PI planning, the various sync meetings, the layered roles, get installed wholesale regardless of whether the organization's coordination problem matches what SAFe was built to solve, producing ceremony overhead that outweighs the coordination it buys. Ask what specific coordination failure a given SAFe ceremony prevents. If the answer is "we don't know, this is just what SAFe says to do," the ceremony is cargo cult and can go. The adoption decision most organizations skip: choosing which pieces to install and which to leave out. Apply only the specific mechanisms that address a named coordination problem, and skip the rest. A framework adopted partially and deliberately produces less overhead than either the full framework or no coordination structure at all. Adopting the framework "properly" because partial adoption feels like doing it wrong, which installs overhead for coordination problems the organization doesn't have, simply because the framework bundles them together with the ones it does. Patterns that show up when process is running on schedule but no longer producing what it's meant to. Ceremonies run on schedule regardless of whether the team can name what each one is currently producing The team has never changed its own process based on a retrospective Story points or velocity get reported upward as if comparable across different teams SAFe ceremonies are followed without anyone able to name the specific coordination failure each one prevents "Being agile" and "following the ceremony calendar" are treated as the same thing by leadership

title: AI Architecture Map
description: Pipeline stage by pipeline stage, from raw documents to a grounded, human-supervised, secured response.
body: Managed platform equivalents, all four clouds Managed model access Managed RAG / knowledge base Agent orchestration Native vector search Custom / self-managed training Guardrails / content safety Document intelligence / ingestion Chunking Embeddings Vector indexing & retrieval Reranking & context assembly Generation / model serving Agent tool layer (MCP) Human-in-the-loop Security & threat model PHI & PII data protection Observability & evaluation Disaster recovery & continuity Capacity & scaling Data lineage & source versioning The same six capabilities the toggle below covers in full depth, summarized here across all four providers at a glance. Use it as a rosetta stone for translating a design conversation across clouds. The depth is in the stages that follow. Bedrock, unified Converse API across model families (Claude, Titan, Llama, Mistral) AI Foundry, Azure OpenAI models plus the Foundry Model Catalog's open-weight options Vertex AI, Gemini-first with third-party and open-weight models via Model Garden OCI Generative AI, native and third-party models Bedrock Knowledge Bases (S3, Confluence, SharePoint sources) AI Search with integrated vectorization, hybrid vector, keyword, and semantic ranking built into the index itself Vertex AI Search (Google Drive, Cloud Storage sources) Generative AI Agents RAG service, integrated vector store and ingestion pipeline built in Bedrock Agents, AgentCore, and Flows AI Foundry Agent Service, built-in tool calling Vertex AI Agent Builder Generative AI Agents, tool and API orchestration built into the same service as RAG pgvector on RDS, or OpenSearch at larger scale AI Search's HNSW vector index, hybrid query mode built in Vertex AI Vector Search, or vector functions inside BigQuery AI Vector Search built into Oracle Database 23ai, or HeatWave GenAI for the MySQL side SageMaker Azure Machine Learning Vertex AI custom training OCI Data Science, paired with GPU-backed AI infrastructure instances Bedrock Guardrails, content filtering and PII redaction built in AI Content Safety, prompt shields and content filtering built in Gemini Safety Settings for content filtering, plus Model Armor as a separate service for prompt injection and sensitive data protection OCI Guardrails: content moderation, prompt injection defense, and PII detection, in Inform or Block mode Model family availability by provider changes fast, and sources published a few months apart often disagree. Confirm the current model catalog and licensing directly with the provider rather than trusting a cached comparison, including this one. Turning raw PDFs, scans, forms, and images into machine-readable structured content: OCR, layout analysis, table and key-value extraction. Textract for OCR, layout, table, and key-value extraction; pair with Comprehend for downstream entity extraction on the recovered text. AI Document Intelligence for OCR, layout, table, and key-value extraction using prebuilt or custom-trained models. AI Content Understanding covers multimodal parsing (image, audio, video) as a Foundry service when documents aren't purely text/table. Document AI, with prebuilt processors for common document types (invoices, IDs, contracts) and a general OCR processor for everything else. Document Understanding for OCR, table, and key-value extraction through prebuilt AI models, customizable for industry-specific extraction needs. The unstructured library or docling for parsing, paired with Tesseract or PaddleOCR for text recognition. For layout-aware extraction, a locally served vision-language model (Qwen-VL, InternVL, or a comparable open-weight multimodal model) handles document QA-style extraction where prebuilt OCR alone isn't enough. Splitting extracted content into retrieval-sized units without breaking semantic units apart. Chunking is orchestration-layer logic that runs in your own code, so this one doesn't change when you switch the toggle above. LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter, embedding-similarity-based semantic chunking, or a managed index's built-in chunking step (Azure AI Search's integrated vectorization skillset is one example) all run identically regardless of which provider or self-hosted stack sits downstream. The choice of algorithm matters far more than the choice of cloud. Converting chunks into vectors for semantic retrieval. Titan Text Embeddings via Bedrock, or Cohere Embed for multilingual needs, billed per token with no separate deployment step. OpenAI embedding models (text-embedding-3-large/small) via Foundry, pay-as-you-go per token or reserved via provisioned throughput for predictable latency at volume. Vertex AI text embedding models, billed per character, with native integration into BigQuery for embedding data already living there. OCI Generative AI embedding models, callable through the same API surface as OCI's generation models. Open-weight embedding models (BGE-large, E5-mistral, Nomic Embed, GTE) served on owned GPUs via Hugging Face Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) or an Infinity server. No per-token bill; cost is amortized GPU time. Storing embeddings for fast approximate nearest-neighbor search, typically combined with keyword search for hybrid retrieval. OpenSearch Service for large-scale ANN search with hybrid BM25 support, or pgvector on RDS/Aurora for teams staying inside an existing Postgres footprint. AI Search: HNSW vector index, hybrid (vector + keyword + semantic ranking) query mode, metadata filters, and ACL-aware secure access baked into the index itself. Vertex AI Vector Search for dedicated ANN at scale, or vector functions inside BigQuery when the data already lives there and a separate index is overhead. AI Vector Search built directly into Oracle Database 23ai, keeping vectors and relational data in one system rather than a separate store. pgvector if you want to stay inside an existing Postgres footprint, or a dedicated vector database (Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus) for larger-scale ANN search with metadata filtering. Hybrid search typically pairs the vector store with OpenSearch/Elasticsearch for BM25, or uses a store with native hybrid support. Re-scoring initial retrieval results with a more precise (and more expensive) model before assembling the final context window. Bedrock's Rerank API offers Amazon Rerank 1.0 and Cohere Rerank 3.5 as managed models, and Bedrock Knowledge Bases can apply reranking inside the retrieval call. Outside Knowledge Bases it's an explicit extra step in your retrieval code, the same pattern as self-hosting one. AI Search's semantic ranker applies a Microsoft-trained cross-encoder as an L2 re-ranking pass over the initial hybrid results, exposed as a query-type option, no separate deployment required. Vertex AI Search includes a ranking API as part of its managed search stack, applying a similar L2 re-ranking pass over initial results. Cohere Rerank models built into the Generative AI service itself, called directly through the RerankText API, available both on-demand and through dedicated clusters. Check the service's current model list for which Rerank version is offered in your region. An open cross-encoder reranker (BGE-reranker, Jina Reranker) served alongside the embedding model, typically on the same TEI/Infinity serving stack, called as an explicit extra step in your retrieval code. Running the language model itself against the assembled, grounded context. Bedrock model deployment: unified Converse API across Claude, Titan, Llama, and Mistral. Provisioned Throughput for predictable latency at volume, on-demand for variable load, plus a batch tier at a discount for non-interactive workloads. AI Foundry model deployment: Azure OpenAI models or the Foundry Model Catalog's open-weight options, on managed online endpoints. Provisioned Throughput Units (PTU) for predictable latency and cost at volume, or pay-as-you-go token billing for variable load. Vertex AI model deployment: Gemini-first, with third-party and open-weight models available through Model Garden. Provisioned throughput and pay-as-you-go both available, same shape as the other two. OCI Generative AI model deployment, native and third-party models, callable through the same managed endpoint pattern as the rest of the OCI Generative AI service. vLLM or TGI serving an open-weight model (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek-class) on owned or leased GPUs, with continuous batching and paged KV-cache for throughput. Ollama for smaller-scale or development use; llama.cpp for CPU/edge deployment. Giving the model controlled access to enterprise systems and external data through defined tools. Bedrock Agents, AgentCore, and Flows for managed tool-use orchestration, or a self-built MCP server fronting enterprise systems, called from a Bedrock-hosted agent. AI Foundry Agent Service with built-in tool calling, or a self-built MCP server fronting enterprise systems, called from a Foundry-hosted agent. Vertex AI Agent Builder for managed tool orchestration, or a self-built MCP server called from a Vertex AI-hosted agent. OCI Generative AI Agents, with tool and API orchestration built into the same service that handles RAG. Identical MCP server code across every environment, since MCP is a protocol rather than a cloud service. The dependency that bites is whether your serving stack (vLLM, TGI) supports the model's native tool-calling chat template, so verify per model rather than assuming. Routing outputs by risk and reversibility to a review queue, notification layer, and durable orchestration that can pause and resume a process for hours or days. DynamoDB for the review queue/state table, SNS or SQS plus EventBridge for notification and escalation timers, Step Functions for the durable orchestration that survives a pause spanning hours or days. Cosmos DB or Azure SQL for the review queue/state table, Teams webhook plus Power Automate for notification and escalation timers, Azure Durable Functions for the durable orchestration that survives a pause spanning hours or days. Firestore for the review queue/state table, Pub/Sub for notification, Cloud Workflows for the durable orchestration spanning the pause. Autonomous Database for the review queue/state table, Notifications service for alerts, OCI Functions chained via Events for the durable orchestration. Postgres for the queue, Slack webhook for notification, Temporal (self-hostable) for durable orchestration. Functionally the same architecture as every column above, different concrete products. Prompt injection, tool-call authorization, and the model supply chain. Data doesn't pass through this once; it applies to every stage above. Bedrock Guardrails runs as a pre-processing gate for content filtering and PII redaction on both input and retrieved content. Tool calls run under IAM roles scoped per agent; Bedrock endpoints sit behind VPC endpoints with public access disabled. AI Content Safety's prompt shields run as a pre-processing gate on both user input and any retrieved or tool-returned content before it reaches the model, since an injected instruction can arrive through a poisoned document just as easily as through the chat box. Tool calls run under managed identities with least-privilege RBAC scoped per agent through Entra ID. Foundry deployments sit behind private endpoints and VNet integration; AI Search restricted to private link with public network access disabled. Two layers: Gemini's built-in Safety Settings for per-request content filtering (hate speech, harassment, sexually explicit, dangerous content, configurable thresholds), plus Model Armor as a separate dedicated service for prompt injection and jailbreak detection, sensitive data protection, and malware scanning. IAM and VPC Service Controls provide the network and identity isolation layer underneath both. OCI Guardrails, a named, documented feature with three protections: content moderation (hate speech, harassment, violence, explicit material), prompt injection defense (binary risk scoring on embedded malicious instructions), and PII detection. Configurable in Inform mode (logs and returns results) or Block mode (rejects the request), available on both on-demand and dedicated cluster endpoints. No managed prompt-shield equivalent. Typically an open guard model (Llama Guard, or a policy layer like NeMo Guardrails) run as a pre and post filter in your own pipeline, tuned and maintained by you. Tool-call authorization is your own implementation at the MCP server layer, commonly OAuth2 or mTLS between the agent runtime and each tool server. Model and weight supply chain matters here specifically: verify checksums and provenance of downloaded weights against the publisher's signed release. Network isolation is your own VPC or on-prem segmentation around the GPU serving cluster. The technical control layer. Policy, accountability, and audit ownership for regulated data live on the AI Governance Map; this is what enforces it in the pipeline. Comprehend Medical and Comprehend's PII detectio

title: AI and the Engineering Operating Model
body: What changes, and what doesn't AI productivity does not automatically equal more story points Code review changes shape What happens to junior engineer development Measuring productivity when the tool is part of the output Signs AI adoption is being measured or managed naively AI-assisted coding shifts specific parts of the job and leaves others alone. Treating it as a uniform speedup misreads what's happening. Changes Doesn't change Speed of first-draft code and boilerplate generation The cost of a wrong architectural decision What code review has to look for Who's accountable for what ships How junior engineers first encounter patterns The need for architectural judgment on anything non-routine Where the bottleneck in the delivery pipeline sits The value of debugging intuition built through direct repetition The most common measurement mistake, and the one most likely to produce a plan that breaks on contact with reality. AI-assisted coding speeds up the mechanical parts, boilerplate, first drafts, syntax, which moves the bottleneck to review, architectural judgment, and testing. Those were never the slow part for a senior engineer, and they were close to the entire job for a junior one. Treating a rise in lines of code or pull request volume as productivity, then setting headcount or delivery expectations against that number. The plan breaks the moment the team hits the bottleneck AI never touched: review capacity and architectural decision-making. Reviewing AI-generated code is a different skill than reviewing human-written code, and most engineers were never trained on the difference. Reviewing AI-generated code means checking for plausible-but-wrong patterns, code that looks idiomatic and compiles cleanly but embeds a subtly incorrect assumption, more than checking for the kind of mistake a human engineer is likely to make. That's a distinct reviewing skill. Review fatigue from higher volume, combined with AI-generated code's tendency to look confident and clean, produces a false sense of safety. Reviewers approve faster because the code reads well, without having verified it any more rigorously. The concern most tempting to dismiss, because it doesn't show up as a problem until much later. A junior engineer who leans on AI for the mechanical work skips the repetition that used to build pattern recognition and debugging intuition the slow way. That intuition doesn't obviously appear missing until a novel problem requires it and it isn't there. Deliberately assign some work without AI assistance specifically for skill-building, framed as a training decision rather than a productivity one, the same way a pilot still trains on manual flight even though autopilot handles most of the flying. The measurement question every other section on this page eventually points back to. Raw output volume: lines of code, pull requests merged, AI suggestions accepted. All of these can rise while the team ships less correct, maintained value, since none of them measure whether the output was right. The outcome measures already covered on Engineering Metrics, cycle time, change failure rate, and ultimately business outcomes, tracked specifically before and after AI tooling adoption, rather than assuming adoption itself is automatically the win. Patterns that show up when AI tooling gets adopted enthusiastically but without adjusting how the organization measures or trains around it. Productivity claims rest on lines of code, PR volume, or AI suggestion acceptance rate rather than outcome measures Code review practice hasn't been adjusted for the specific failure modes of AI-generated code No deliberate mechanism exists for junior engineers to build skills without AI assistance Change failure rate or defect rate hasn't been tracked before and after AI tooling adoption Headcount or timeline plans assume a productivity multiplier that was asserted rather than measured

title: AI FinOps Map
description: Cost modeling stage by stage across AWS, Azure, GCP, OCI, and self-hosted, the same environments the Architecture Map covers in depth.
body: Pricing model: tokens vs amortized hardware Find your own break-even point Reserved capacity vs GPU procurement Chargeback & unit economics Cost observability & budget alerting Model selection as a cost lever Waste: idle reservations and orphaned capacity Prompt caching Batch / asynchronous processing The fundamental cost shape differs before any workload-specific decisions get made. Bedrock is billed per token, input and output priced separately, output typically several times more expensive than input, with per-model rates spanning roughly $0.035 to $10 per million input tokens depending on model tier. Cost scales directly and immediately with usage, unpredictable at the account level until volume stabilizes. Pay-as-you-go is billed per token, input and output priced separately, output typically several times more expensive than input. Cost scales directly and immediately with usage, visible per-call, but unpredictable at the account level until volume stabilizes. Vertex AI bills current Gemini models per token, input and output metered separately; older model generations were metered per character, so check which meter applies to the model you pick. An easy-to-miss cost multiplier: Gemini's internal reasoning (thinking) tokens are billed as output, and on reasoning-heavy requests they can inflate cost several times beyond what the visible response length suggests. On-demand OCI Generative AI is billed per transaction (character-based) for on-demand inference, separate from the per-unit-hour rate that applies once you move to a dedicated cluster. Consumption draws against an existing Universal Credits commitment rather than a standalone bill. Cost is amortized GPU time (purchase or lease depreciation, power, cooling, ops staff), largely fixed regardless of query volume until you hit a capacity ceiling and need to add hardware. Marginal cost per additional query approaches zero until that ceiling, then jumps in a large step when you provision another node. The formula above, made concrete. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. Committing ahead of time to guarantee throughput and control cost variance. Provisioned Throughput reserves dedicated capacity in model units, billed hourly whether used or not, at roughly $24 to $200 per hour depending on model. Only pays off above sustained utilization; buying a 6-month commitment before traffic is stable is the single fastest way to overspend here. Some custom and fine-tuned models still require Provisioned Throughput rather than on-demand billing; check the deployment options for the specific model before assuming pay-as-you-go is available. Provisioned Throughput Units (PTU) reserve dedicated capacity at a flat monthly rate, converting variable token cost into a predictable fixed cost, but only pays off above a specific utilization threshold; idle PTU capacity is money spent on nothing. Provisioned throughput, priced per generative scale unit hour rather than per token, with 20 to 45 percent savings available via 1-month or 1-year commitments. Break-even against on-demand typically lands around $50 a day in sustained spend on a single model; below that, on-demand usually wins. Dedicated AI clusters bill per unit-hour, but the distinctive gotcha here is the minimum commitment: hosting clusters require at least 744 unit-hours, roughly a full month, even if actual usage is far lower. That minimum doesn't exist on the other three clouds' reserved-capacity tiers. Owning or leasing GPUs is the hardware equivalent of a reserved-capacity commitment: a large fixed cost that only pays off at sustained utilization. Renting from a GPU cloud (on-demand) is the hardware equivalent of pay-as-you-go, more expensive per hour but no idle-capacity risk. Making AI spend attributable to the team or product that generated it instead of leaving it as one opaque line item. Cost Explorer's tagging and cost allocation tags attribute Bedrock spend to a team, product, or environment tag, feeding a per-team chargeback model the same way any other AWS resource would. Cost Management's tagging and scope hierarchy lets you attribute Foundry deployment spend to a subscription, resource group, or tag, feeding a per-team or per-product chargeback model the same way any other Azure resource would. Cloud Billing labels plus BigQuery billing export let you attribute Vertex AI spend down to the label or project level, queryable alongside the rest of the GCP bill rather than as an isolated line item. Compartment structure plus tag-based attribution in OCI Cost Analysis, with FOCUS-format billing exports increasingly the default pipeline for feeding a chargeback model. Cost Analysis falls back to a tagless view when tag coverage is incomplete. No managed billing hierarchy to lean on; attribution requires your own request-tagging at the application layer (which team or product initiated the call) correlated against GPU-hour cost allocated proportionally to usage. This is meaningfully more engineering work to build. Catching a cost anomaly (a runaway agent loop, a misconfigured retry, a prompt that ballooned in size) before the monthly bill does. AWS Budgets with configurable thresholds and Cost Anomaly Detection using machine learning to flag unusual spend patterns automatically, without a manually defined rule for every scenario. Cost Management budgets with action-group-triggered alerts at defined thresholds; Monitor can alert on token consumption rate directly if instrumented, catching an anomaly within the billing period rather than after it closes. Budgets & Alerts plus Cost Anomaly Detection at the billing-account level; the reasoning-token cost multiplier from Stage 1 is exactly the kind of anomaly this catches before it compounds across a month of traffic. OCI Cost Analysis with budget-based alerts, increasingly paired with FOCUS-format billing exports for teams that have moved off the native dashboard onto a broader FinOps pipeline. No native billing-anomaly alerting since there's no per-token bill to watch. The equivalent signal is GPU utilization and request-rate anomalies via Prometheus alerting. An unusual spike in request volume or output length is the leading indicator you have. The single highest-leverage FinOps decision, made once per use case, before any of the above matters. Bedrock's catalog spans roughly $0.035 to $10 per million input tokens across model tiers; routing simple classification or extraction tasks to a cheaper model (Nova Micro or Haiku-class) and reserving the frontier model for complex reasoning is often a larger lever than any reservation optimization. Foundry's model catalog spans a wide price-performance range; routing simple classification or extraction tasks to a smaller, cheaper model and reserving the frontier model for complex reasoning is often a larger cost lever than any PTU or reservation optimization. Gemini Flash-Lite at roughly $0.10/$0.40 per million tokens versus Pro-tier pricing several times higher; the same routing principle applies, with the added wrinkle that reasoning tokens make the effective cost gap between tiers larger than the sticker price alone suggests. OCI's catalog spans Oracle-curated and partner models (Cohere, Llama, xAI Grok) at meaningfully different price points; the same routing principle applies, and dedicated-cluster pricing tiers differ enough by model family that the choice compounds with the reserved-capacity decision from Stage 2. Same principle, and arguably higher stakes: a smaller open-weight model (7B to 14B class) served efficiently can handle a large share of production traffic at a fraction of the GPU footprint a frontier-class open-weight model requires, if the task doesn't need frontier reasoning. The unglamorous but highest-frequency cost leak across every environment. Provisioned Throughput reserved for peak load sitting idle most of the day; forgotten Knowledge Bases vector storage (OpenSearch Serverless bills a minimum around $345/month even at zero query traffic) left running after a project ends. Both invisible unless someone is specifically auditing deployed resources against active use cases. PTU reservations sized for peak load sitting idle most of the day; forgotten dev/test Foundry deployments left running after the project using them ended. Both invisible unless someone is specifically auditing deployed resources against actual active use cases. Online prediction endpoints, Vector Search nodes, and Workbench instances all bill per hour regardless of traffic; a forgotten deployed endpoint is one of the most common GCP AI cost surprises, silently running up thousands a month for zero real usage. Idle dedicated AI clusters are described directly in Oracle's own licensing guidance as the top cost trap: a reserved cluster bills around the clock, and under-utilized, can cost many times what on-demand inference would for the same volume, compounded by the 744-hour minimum commitment from Stage 2. GPU nodes provisioned for a launch that never reached expected volume, or a dev cluster left running after the project wound down. Same failure mode, higher absolute cost per incident since GPU hardware commitments are larger and stickier than a cloud service you can just delete. A cost lever specific to how LLMs are billed, with no equivalent in traditional cloud FinOps. Prompt caching on Bedrock caches a stable prefix (system prompt, long reference document) and bills the cached portion at roughly 10 percent of the standard input rate, up to 90 percent savings on context-heavy applications. Same architectural discipline as every provider here: stable content first, dynamic content last, or the cache never hits. Repeated prompt prefixes above a minimum length get served from cache automatically on Standard deployments, at a steep discount, commonly in the 50 to 90 percent range on the cached portion, no client-side opt-in required. The architectural work is keeping the cacheable part of the prompt byte-identical and in the same position on every request; dynamic content has to move to the end, after the cacheable prefix, or the cache never hits. Context caching stores a repeated prompt prefix at a steep discount, commonly cited around 75 to 90 percent off the cached portion depending on source, plus a separate storage charge billed per character per hour the cache is held. Worth checking current figures directly since sources disagree on the exact discount rate. As of this review, OCI does not document a general-purpose prompt caching discount comparable to the other three clouds. Treat this lever as unavailable on OCI until Oracle publishes one, and re-check before a renewal. vLLM and most modern serving stacks support prefix caching (often called automatic prefix caching or APC) natively, and the same discipline applies: stable content first, dynamic content last. The saving shows up as GPU time not spent recomputing the same prefix, rather than a line-item discount on a bill, so it has to be measured through throughput and latency metrics instead of a cost dashboard. Trading latency for a flat discount, available whenever the workload can tolerate a delayed result. Batch Inference processes a submitted job asynchronously at 50 percent off standard on-demand pricing. Batch doesn't support tool calling, structured output, or multi-turn conversation, so it is a different execution model rather than a slower version of the same one. Don't move an agent loop to Batch because the token price is lower. The Batch API processes a submitted job asynchronously, typically within a 24-hour target, at roughly 50 percent off standard pay-as-you-go pricing. Useful for nightly document processing, bulk content generation, embeddings refreshes, and model evaluations. Not usable for interactive chat or any customer-facing path expecting an immediate response. Gemini batch prediction runs non-urgent jobs asynchronously at roughly 50 percent off standard token rates within a 24-hour target. One gotcha applies to batch prediction on custom-trained models rather than Gemini: Google bills for the provisioned cluster runtime rather than active processing time, so under-filled jobs cost more per prediction than expected. Batching requests into larger groups is the fix. As of this review, OCI does not document an asynchronous batch-discount tier comparable to the other three clouds. Treat this lever as unavailable on OCI until Oracle publishes one, and re-check before a renewal. The equivalent move is scheduling batch workloads for off-peak GPU capacity, or running them through the same continuous-batching serving stack at a lower priority queue than interactive traffic. There's no separate billed rate to point to. The saving comes from higher GPU utilization on hardware that would otherwise sit idle overnight, which still has to be measured to know it's happening.

title: AI Governance Map
description: Four layers, from data foundation to responsible AI oversight, each with concrete controls mapped to what breaks without them and which regulatory frameworks.
body: Data foundation Governance layer Trusted outputs Responsible AI & high-risk oversight Model risk management The standards and credentials landscape Is ISO 42001 certification worth pursuing Regulatory framework mapping Accountability & audit trail AI-specific incident response Before anything else, know what the model uses. If you cannot answer where a piece of training or retrieval data came from, nothing above this layer holds up. Source registry covering every system feeding the AI pipeline Data dictionary defining what each field means and where it originated Lineage and provenance tracking from source document to retrieved chunk Clear data ownership assigned per source system NIST AI RMF's Map function starts here: you cannot assess risk in a system whose inputs you cannot trace. Without this layer, an incident investigation cannot answer "where did this bad output come from," which is usually the first question an investigation asks. Once the data foundation is solid, decide who decides what. Definition locks, retrieval boundaries, input validation, and a named data steward give the system clear lines of accountability. Definition locks: agreed, versioned definitions for terms the system reasons about, so they stop drifting between teams Retrieval boundaries: which sources an agent or index is allowed to draw from for a given use case Input validation on both user prompts and any document entering the ingestion pipeline A named data steward with the authority to change what's retrievable Without a data steward, retrieval boundaries erode silently as new sources get connected for convenience, and the system starts answering from data nobody approved for that use case. This is the layer that turns "we have a RAG pipeline" into "we have a RAG pipeline someone is accountable for." With governance in place, you can start defending your answers. Confidence thresholds, output guardrails, and bias checks turn "the AI said so" into something you can stand behind to a customer, auditor, or regulator. Confidence thresholds tied to the human-in-the-loop tiering model (see the Architecture Map) Output guardrails: schema validation, citation requirements, forbidden-content checks before a response ships Bias and fairness checks on outputs for any use case touching people (hiring, credit, care recommendations) Explainability sufficient to answer "why did it say that" after the fact, as well as at design time A confidence score without a documented threshold policy is a number nobody acts on consistently, and no auditor will accept it as a control. This layer is what regulators and auditors ask to see evidence of, so it has to produce artifacts (logs, rubric scores) rather than exist only as a design intention. The outer layer: autonomous agents, high-risk decisions, and regulated use cases. This only works because everything underneath it is already solid. Formal classification of which use cases count as high-risk under applicable frameworks Documented incident response plan specific to AI failures, separate from the generic IT incident process Human oversight for high-risk decisions, implemented as the Tier 2 gate described on the Architecture Map and enforced in code rather than by policy statement alone Hallucination and groundedness checks running continuously in production, beyond the initial launch evaluation Credit scoring, employment screening, and medical decisioning fall within the EU AI Act's Annex III high-risk use cases when the specific system matches the criteria listed there; operating in one of those domains does not by itself make a system high-risk. Article 14 requires human oversight for systems that do qualify. The high-risk obligations were deferred by the Digital Omnibus on AI, adopted in June 2026 and in force from 27 July 2026: Annex III stand-alone systems, including employment and credit uses, now apply from 2 December 2027, and AI embedded in Annex I regulated products from 2 August 2028. Article 50 transparency duties still apply from 2 August 2026. The final text set fixed dates and dropped the Commission's earlier proposal to tie them to the readiness of harmonised standards, so confirm the current date for your specific use case against the published regulation. Treating the model itself, and not only its outputs, as something with a lifecycle that needs governing. A model inventory listing every deployed model, its version, what it's used for, and who owns the decision to keep using it. Pre-deployment evaluation against a defined rubric before a new model version replaces an old one. Ongoing drift monitoring in production, tied to the observability stage on the Architecture Map, in place of a one-time evaluation at launch. The single most common gap: a team can name the model they deployed in January but not confirm what's running in production today after three silent provider-side updates. If you cannot answer "which exact model version produced this output," you cannot investigate an incident or defend a decision. Four different things people mean when they say "AI governance," easy to conflate and different in what they certify, who holds them, and what they cost. Name What it is Who or what it applies to AIGP (IAPP) An individual professional credential, the AI-governance equivalent of IAPP's CIPP privacy certifications. 100-question exam across four domains: AI governance foundations, applicable laws and standards, governing AI development, governing AI deployment and use. A person. Validates that someone can run an AI governance program; doesn't certify the organization or any specific system. ISO/IEC 42001 A certifiable AI management system standard, the AI equivalent of ISO 27001 for information security. Third-party audited (Stage 1 and Stage 2), valid three years with annual surveillance audits, 38 Annex A controls selected and justified against your own risk assessment rather than applied as a fixed checklist. An organization's AI management system. Already held by AWS, Anthropic, and Microsoft. Doesn't by itself satisfy EU AI Act obligations, but the risk assessment and governance structure it requires feeds directly into the technical documentation the Act does require. NIST AI RMF A voluntary US framework (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage). It is guidance to structure a program against; nobody audits you to it. An organization's practice, self-assessed. Already referenced throughout this page's layer structure. ISO/IEC 23894 Risk management guidance specific to AI, meant to be used alongside ISO 31000's general risk management approach. An organization's risk process. Guidance rather than a certifiable standard on its own. OECD AI Principles High-level international principles (inclusive growth, human-centered values, transparency, robustness, accountability), adopted by dozens of governments as policy language. National policy and regulation that draws on these principles; not something an organization implements or gets certified against directly. A decision with a cost attached. Don't default into it because the standard exists. Enterprise customers or regulators are asking for independent evidence of AI governance maturity and a policy document no longer satisfies them. Selling into procurement processes where a competitor's ISO 42001 badge is becoming a checkbox. The organization already holds ISO 27001, since the incremental cost and timeline drop substantially when the management-system muscle already exists. A small AI footprint with a handful of internal use cases and no customer demanding third-party evidence. The four layers above aren't solidly in place yet. Certifying a management system before the underlying technical controls exist produces a certificate that doesn't reflect reality, and an auditor will eventually find that gap. NIST AI RMF, applied seriously and evidenced internally, covers most of the same ground without the $20,000 to $60,000 audit cost and multi-year commitment. Which control layer above satisfies which framework's requirement. Not legal advice; confirm applicability with counsel for your specific use case and jurisdiction. Framework What it requires Which layer covers it HIPAA Minimum necessary access, immutable audit trail for PHI access Layer 2 (retrieval boundaries) plus the PHI/PII stage on the Architecture Map EU AI Act, Article 14 Human oversight for high-risk AI systems Layer 4, enforced technically via the HITL tiering model NIST AI RMF Govern, Map, Measure, Manage functions across the AI lifecycle All four layers plus model risk management, roughly one NIST function per layer ISO/IEC 42001 An auditable AI management system: policy, risk assessment, selected Annex A controls, continuous improvement All four layers plus the accountability and model risk management sections provide the evidence an auditor asks for SOC 2 (if applicable to the AI system) Access controls, change management, monitoring evidence Layer 2 for access, model risk management for change control, Layer 3 for monitoring evidence Who signs off on an AI system going live, and what gets logged so that decision can be reconstructed later. A named accountable owner per AI use case. A committee with no single decision-maker does not count. Decision logging: every promotion of a new model or index version recorded with who approved it and what evaluation evidence supported the approval. Diffuse accountability is a recurring AI governance failure pattern behind headline incidents. It's rarely that no one thought about the risk; it's that no single person owned the decision to accept it. Different from a general IT incident: a hallucinated answer causing harm, a bias incident, or a model behaving unexpectedly needs its own triage path. A defined severity classification specific to AI failures (harmful hallucination, biased output, data leakage through a response, agent taking an unauthorized action). A rollback path that can revert to a prior model or index version quickly, which depends directly on the versioning discipline described in model risk management above. A general incident response process (see Incident Response) usually isn't built to ask "was this the model's fault, the retrieval's fault, or the underlying data's fault," and that triage question determines the fix. Build this as an extension of the general process rather than a replacement for it.

title: AI Portfolio Management
description: Which AI initiatives should get built, scored and classified with the same discipline applied to the rest of the application estate.
body: Scoring dimensions and classification Feasibility and data readiness gate the score before anything else contributes to it Reversibility deserves its own weight Kill criteria set before the bet starts Score an initiative Signs AI portfolio governance isn't real Nine dimensions feed the score; four classifications follow from it. The value is in forcing the same questions to be asked of every initiative, so the loudest pitch can't skip the screen. Precision in the score itself matters less. Dimension What it asks Business value What outcome does this move, and how much Feasibility Can this be built with current capability and technology Data readiness Does the required data exist, at the needed quality, with clear rights to use it Risk Regulatory, reputational, and model-behavior risk if this goes wrong Adoption likelihood Will the people this is built for use it Time to value How long until the outcome in row one is realized, which is a later date than launch Operating cost The ongoing cost to run this, on top of the cost to build it Differentiation Does this create an advantage competitors can't quickly copy Reversibility How expensive is it to unwind this if it doesn't work out Classification Meaning Scale Proven value and feasibility; fund it fully and remove obstacles Incubate Promising but unproven on one or more dimensions; fund a bounded pilot with a defined checkpoint Watch Not ready to fund, but conditions could change; revisit on a set schedule rather than forgetting about it Kill Fails on a gating dimension or has passed its own kill criteria; stop funding it explicitly and say so Averaging all nine dimensions into one number lets a high-value, technically infeasible idea pass through if it scores generously elsewhere. Screen on feasibility and data readiness first. If the data doesn't exist at usable quality, or the model risk is unacceptable regardless of upside, the initiative doesn't reach a business-value conversation at all. Gating dimensions eliminate; they don't get averaged away. A compelling business case with a fatal data gap can still produce a respectable average score if the other eight dimensions are strong, which is exactly how organizations end up funding pilots that were never going to work, discovered only after real money and credibility were spent. Not all AI bets carry the same downside if they fail, and the classification should reflect that. A pilot built on a vendor API is cheap to unwind. A model embedded into a core workflow customers now depend on is expensive to unwind. Two initiatives with identical business-value scores warrant different treatment if one is trivially reversible and the other isn't. Treating an irreversible bet with the same enthusiasm as a reversible pilot because both scored well on value, without ever separately asking what it costs to walk away if the initial results don't hold up at scale. AI initiatives are unusually prone to surviving on prestige rather than results, which makes advance kill criteria more important here than almost anywhere else in the portfolio. Define, before funding, the specific result that would trigger a move to Watch or Kill, a metric, a threshold, a date. Write it down where it can't be quietly renegotiated once the team is emotionally invested in the outcome. An initiative that's been "six months from proving itself" for over a year, kept alive because killing an AI project carries a different kind of organizational embarrassment than killing an ordinary feature, independent of what the results show. Score all nine dimensions 1 to 5. Feasibility and data readiness are hard gates; a low score on either kills the initiative regardless of everything else. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. Patterns that show up when AI initiatives are being funded by momentum rather than by the same discipline applied elsewhere in the technology portfolio. No AI initiative has ever been formally moved to Kill despite some producing no measurable result Feasibility and data readiness were never checked before funding, only the business case The same initiative has been described as close to proving itself for well over a year No one can name what's currently in Watch status or when it's due for reassessment AI investment decisions bypass the standard capital allocation process applied to everything else

title: Application Portfolio Management
body: What exists behind this preview Technical debt backlog Application risk register Portfolio classification (TIME) M&A-specific variant The Gartner TIME model, applied Risk as an independent axis, kept out of the TIME inputs Turning individual scores into a portfolio signal Debt, risk, and application portfolio simulator TIME quadrant classifier A working spreadsheet instrument rather than a static framework: three linked sheets feeding one dashboard, with the same scoring logic reused for standing portfolio governance and for scoring an acquisition target's stack under diligence. 3 linked sheets · 1 live dashboard · standing portfolio and M&A variants Every known debt item scored on severity, business impact, confidence, and remediation effort, rolled up to a priority ranking. Direct remediation, annual carry, and contingent risk cost per item, each carrying its own confidence rating Status and aging tracked against a target remediation window, so stale items surface instead of hiding Rolls into portfolio-level totals: active items by severity, cost by confidence tier, overdue count A five-factor risk score per application, independent of how valuable or well-built the system is. Cybersecurity, compliance, operational resilience, vendor, and knowledge-concentration risk scored separately, then composited Surfaces the application that's fine on paper but one departure or one vendor lapse from a bad quarter Every application placed on the Gartner TIME grid using a Business Value score and a Technical Health score. Business Value built from five factors: strategic alignment, business criticality, user reach, differentiation, regulatory necessity Technical Health built from five factors: technology currency, architecture quality, integration complexity, data architecture fit, technical debt Composite Portfolio Score, cost score, and risk score sit alongside the classification as informational overlays and are kept out of its inputs The same instrument, repointed at a target company's application estate during diligence or the first 100 days. Same scoring mechanics, framed around acquisition-specific questions: what's redundant with the acquirer's stack, what's a hidden Eliminate candidate the seller never flagged Feeds directly into the Integration Architecture Decision Tree's merge, integrate, or coexist call per system Every application lands in one of four quadrants based on two independent scores: how much the business needs it, and how healthy it is technically. Invest: high value, high health. Fund it. Tolerate: low value, high health. Leave it alone and don't over-invest. Migrate: high value, low health. This is the modernization backlog, ranked by value at risk. Eliminate: low value, low health. These are the retirement candidates most portfolios carry more of than anyone admits. Business Value gets inflated when the scorer is the system's own owner. Score it with someone outside the owning team in the room, or the whole portfolio drifts toward Invest and the model stops doing its job. Technical Health is the opposite failure: engineers score their own systems harshly relative to peers they haven't had to maintain, which skews Migrate counts up. A system can be a clean Invest on the TIME grid and still be the one that takes the company down. Risk is scored and reported separately on purpose. Folding risk into Technical Health hides exactly the applications that need visibility: strategically critical, well-funded, actively developed, and sitting on a single unreplaceable engineer or an end-of-life dependency no one has scheduled work against. Reporting risk on its own axis keeps that combination visible instead of averaging it away. These get remediation budget ahead of Migrate-quadrant systems, even though they score well overall, because the downside is asymmetric: a breach or a key-person departure on a high-value system costs more than slow modernization debt on a low-value one. One application's score is a data point. The value is in the aggregate: how many Eliminate candidates are still costing money, how concentrated the high-risk applications are, whether Migrate is growing or shrinking quarter over quarter. Average Composite Portfolio Score by quadrant, count of high-risk applications, count of high-cost applications relative to their Business Value, and the ratio of Eliminate-classified applications still consuming a meaningful share of total run cost. Movement in these over two or three quarters tells you whether governance is changing behavior or only producing a nicer chart. Treating this as a one-time inventory exercise. A TIME classification from eighteen months ago is closer to fiction than to data; technical health decays continuously even when business value hasn't moved, so the cadence matters as much as the scoring model itself. One workbook for the three registers this page describes: a debt backlog with severity, impact, confidence, and effort scoring plus direct, carry, and contingent cost; a risk register across cybersecurity, compliance, resilience, vendor, and knowledge concentration; and an application portfolio that scores business value, cost, and technical health, classifies each application on the TIME quadrant, and rolls up to an overview dashboard. Room for a thousand rows in each, with sample data loaded. Scoring weights are on the Lists sheet at even defaults so you can see and change them. The calibrated weights by industry and the M&A target-scoring variant are part of the full simulator, available through direct engagement. Score one application on the same five-factor Business Value and Technical Health axes the full instrument uses. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. Risk and cost scoring, and the multi-application portfolio view, are part of the full simulator.

title: Architecture Principles Library
body: What makes a principle worth having Buy before build, build only where differentiation justifies the cost Pay down technical debt continuously instead of in campaigns Make reversible decisions quickly; reserve slow deliberation for the irreversible Prefer loose coupling between autonomous teams over tight integration Failure is the default state; design for it Observability is a first-class concern Prefer convention over configuration; prefer explicit over implicit Automate what gets done more than twice Data has one authoritative source; every other copy is derived from it Data models reflect domain reality rather than system convenience Classify data by sensitivity before any other decision The team that builds runs, or the runbook doesn't exist Decisions are recorded; rationale is part of the decision Small, stable teams outperform large, dynamic ones for complex work Measure what matters; do not optimize what is merely easy to measure Conflict is expected Most architecture principles are bad: generic ("we will be agile"), self-serving ("we prefer our favorite technology"), or untestable ("we will deliver business value"). A useful principle has four properties. Names a specific trade-off the organization has chosen Is defensible against its opposite Produces different decisions than its absence would Comes with examples of when it was applied and what was given up as a result Rationale: Most software the organization needs has already been built by someone else. Building it again produces ongoing maintenance costs for software that doesn't differentiate the business. Trade-off: Loss of control over roadmap and feature set. Accepted for commodity capabilities, rejected for differentiating ones. Worked example: Customer identity management is commodity, adopt a commercial platform. Fraud detection for a specific transaction pattern is differentiating, build it. Signs of misapplication: Everything gets classified as differentiating to justify building. The cure is making someone name the differentiation concretely. Rationale: Debt accumulates continuously. Campaigns to address it are always disruptive, under-scoped, and insufficient. Trade-off: Feature velocity appears lower in the short term because capacity is visibly allocated away from new work. Worked example: Delivery teams allocate 15 to 20 percent of sprint capacity to debt items, owned by engineering, informed to product. Signs of misapplication: The allocation becomes theoretical; sprint reviews consistently show 100 percent feature work. Rationale: Treating all decisions with the same process produces either dangerous speed on the irreversible or pointless bureaucracy on the reversible. Trade-off: Some decisions are harder to classify than the principle implies; the organization has to develop judgment about what's reversible in its context. Worked example: A logging library choice is reversible, the team picks and moves. A primary data platform can't be reversed within a reasonable timeframe, so it goes through review with ADR documentation. Signs of misapplication: Teams classify inconvenient decisions as irreversible to defer them, or reversible to avoid oversight. The test: what does it cost in time and money to change this in 18 months? Rationale: Tight coupling between systems produces tight coupling between the teams that own them, and destroys both the system's and the team's autonomy over time. Trade-off: Loose coupling costs more to build initially; interfaces take design effort that a shared database doesn't. Worked example: The Order team calls the Customer service's API rather than reading the Customer database directly. The Customer team can refactor storage without coordinating with Order. Signs of misapplication: Teams paper over coupling with facades that still expose the underlying structure. Test: if the upstream team changes its implementation, does the downstream code break? Rationale: At any non-trivial scale, something is always failing. Systems designed on the assumption that components work experience their first failure as an outage. Trade-off: Upfront complexity; designing for failure takes thought and adds code paths. Worked example: The order placement service, when the fraud service is unavailable, falls back to rule-based scoring rather than refusing orders. Flagged orders get deferred review. Signs of misapplication: Retries and fallbacks added without thinking through cascade effects; retry storms that take down dependencies are worse than the original failure. Rationale: Systems not designed to be observed are systems whose behavior is a mystery in production, and the cost of instrumenting retroactively is higher than instrumenting from the start. Trade-off: Instrumentation is code that must be maintained; noisy instrumentation is worse than none. Worked example: Every service produces request logs with correlation IDs, metrics on the operations that matter most, and traces covering cross-service flows, specified alongside functional requirements. Signs of misapplication: Teams log everything, measure nothing, and produce dashboards nobody reads. The cure: for each piece of instrumentation, ask what decision it supports. Rationale: Configuration without convention produces infinite surface area. Convention without explicit seams produces invisible magic. Trade-off: The organization must invest in establishing and evolving conventions, ongoing work that drifts into inconsistency without it. Worked example: All services log in a common format and expose health/metrics on conventional paths. A service deviating for regulatory reasons documents why, explicitly. Signs of misapplication: Conventions are stated but not enforced; new services do whatever their authors prefer. Rationale: Manual work is error-prone, non-repeatable, and invisible. The person doing it is a bottleneck and a knowledge concentration point. Trade-off: Automation costs more than doing the thing once; the 'more than twice' rule calibrates when that cost is worth paying. Worked example: New developer environment setup was a 3-day manual process. After the second hire it became a script; after the fifth, a one-click pipeline. Signs of misapplication: Automation becomes an end in itself; teams automate one-off work and produce scripts no one else uses. Rationale: Parallel sources of truth always diverge, usually not discovered until a reconciliation problem surfaces in production. Trade-off: The authoritative source becomes a hard dependency for every downstream consumer; its availability matters more than in a distributed-truth design. Worked example: Customer contact information is authoritative in the CRM; Marketing receives it via streaming replica; Billing queries CRM directly. Nobody has their own editable copy. Signs of misapplication: Two teams claim authoritative ownership of overlapping data; reconciliation scripts appear. The cure is naming a single owner and migrating the other to consumer status. Rationale: Data outlives systems. A model shaped by today's storage technology will be wrong when the technology changes, which it will. Trade-off: Domain-driven models are sometimes less efficient for the current storage technology than technology-optimized ones would be. Worked example: The order model captures business concepts, order, line item, party, event, because those concepts are stable, regardless of the underlying storage engine. Signs of misapplication: The model has fields named for technical conventions (is_deleted, legacy_status_code) that pollute the domain. The cure is separating domain model from storage model. Rationale: Retrofitting sensitivity controls is more expensive than building them in; systems that move data without awareness of sensitivity produce the gaps that show up in breach postmortems. Trade-off: Classification requires ongoing organizational discipline, every system handling data must know what classification applies. Worked example: Customer purchase history is classified Restricted. A log entry including purchase history is subject to Restricted-level controls even if the producing system wouldn't otherwise be. Signs of misapplication: Classification exists on paper but isn't wired into any control. The cure is instrumenting classification into specific enforcement (encryption, access logging). Rationale: Build-only teams produce systems that are hard to operate because they don't experience the operational cost; run-only teams receive systems they can't confidently change. Trade-off: Asking build teams to operate adds ongoing work. The cost of operational-ownership confusion is larger, but this is still a cost. Worked example: A product team building a customer-facing service is on-call for it. If responsibility transfers to a central ops team, the transfer includes validated runbooks and paired on-call for 90 days. Signs of misapplication: Teams claim to operate but delegate incidents upward constantly. The cure is staffing and training to the operational responsibility. Softening the principle only hides the gap. Rationale: The reasoning behind a decision is usually the most valuable artifact, and the one most frequently lost. Trade-off: Writing a good rationale takes effort, and most teams underestimate how much. Worked example: An event-driven integration decision is recorded as an ADR including alternatives considered, why the chosen path won, and what would trigger revisiting it. Signs of misapplication: ADRs exist but are written as announcements rather than reasoning. 'We will use X' with no explanation of what was rejected is a memo. Rationale: Architectural work compounds on team context. A team that's operated a system for two years makes better decisions about it than one assembled three weeks ago. Trade-off: Stable teams are harder to scale up rapidly for new initiatives; the organization has to plan for this rather than throwing people at problems. Worked example: The team owning customer identity has a core of four engineers with two-plus years on it. New engineers onboard over three to six months rather than three weeks. Signs of misapplication: Team composition changes frequently, no one's been on the team more than six months. The cure is slowing the churn. Asking teams to document more treats the symptom. Rationale: Goodhart's law applies to architecture: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Easy proxies produce organizations that look healthy while failing at what matters. Trade-off: Measures that matter are harder to collect and slower to move; the temptation to substitute easy proxies is constant. Worked example: Instead of 'reviews conducted,' measure 'percentage of significant initiatives with early architecture engagement,' which requires judgment but reflects reality. Signs of misapplication: Dashboards show green metrics while the function is widely considered unhelpful. The cure: ask what consumers of the work would say is getting better or worse. Principles conflict. The conflict surfaces a trade-off the organization has to make; three approaches help resolve it in practice. State the specific conflict. "These sometimes conflict" is useless; "P1 conflicts with P4 here because the commercial product creates tight coupling with our existing systems" is resolvable. Identify which principle the context prioritizes. A regulatory system might privilege data classification over decision speed; a greenfield product might privilege the reverse. Neither is wrong; the context decides. Record the resolution in the ADR. Future decisions in similar contexts have precedent to draw on.

title: Architecture Review Board
body: What belongs in front of the board, and what doesn't Evidence over drawings Setting it up: composition and authority The review itself Running it long-term without decaying into theater Empty slots: turn them into innovation salons instead of canceling Signs the board has become theater The most common way a review board fails is reviewing everything, which turns it into a bottleneck and trains teams to route around it. The same filter used to decide when a decision needs an ADR applies here. Goes to the board Doesn't need the board A new external dependency or a shared service other teams will depend on A team's fully contained internal implementation detail A decision that affects more than one team's roadmap A reversible, single-team decision costing less than a day to undo A new system of record or data store other systems will read from Adding a field to a schema the team already owns exclusively A deliberate deviation from an established architecture principle Following a pattern the board has already approved elsewhere The distinction that separates a review with teeth from a rubber stamp with a diagram attached. The running system, observed traffic patterns, incident history, a working prototype or spike, existing code. Evidence produced by doing the engineering work rather than evidence produced to satisfy the meeting. A polished architecture diagram produced in the days before the review, disconnected from the codebase, that nobody consults again once the meeting ends. The tell: check the diagram file's last-modified date six months later. If it's the review date, it was never a working artifact. Two decisions made once, at founding, that determine whether the board has standing or only a name. A small standing group, four to six people, spanning the systems most likely to be affected by cross-cutting decisions. Rotate membership on a defined cycle so it doesn't calcify into the same five people's opinions indefinitely. The proposing team's own senior engineer is always in the room, never reviewed in absentia. See Technology Decision Rights: the board should be Consulted, rarely Accountable. A named individual, the CTO or a delegate, is accountable for architecture standards and can be persuaded by a strong board recommendation, but the board's vote is input to that person's decision and can be overridden. What makes a specific session evidence-based rather than theater, independent of how well the board was set up. The proposing team walks through the tradeoffs they considered and rejected, the same alternatives-considered discipline covered on the ADR page, with numbers behind claims (this handles X load, this costs Y) rather than assertions. The review produces a decision and its reasoning captured in an ADR. A verbal thumbs-up disappears when the meeting ends. The review becomes a presentation the team already knows how to pass: confident language and a clean diagram calibrated to satisfy the audience rather than stress-test the reasoning. At that point the board is a rubber stamp with theater added, arguably worse than no review, since it spends time producing a false signal of scrutiny. A board that works well in its first year and quietly stops working in its third is the most common lifecycle, and it's predictable enough to design against. A standing cadence, biweekly is common, that runs whether or not there's a full docket. A public backlog of upcoming reviews so teams plan around it instead of being surprised. Periodic retrospectives on the board's own past decisions: did what it approved work out, was what it blocked right to block. The board approves the same rubber-stamp pattern for months. Membership never rotates, so the room's authority rests on tenure rather than current context. No one checks whether a past decision held up, so the board never learns whether its own judgment is any good, and keeps operating on the same instincts regardless of outcomes. What to do with a scheduled review slot that has nothing queued for it, which happens regularly once a board is running well and teams aren't manufacturing proposals just to fill the docket. Instead of canceling the slot, which trains people to deprioritize the cadence, or filling it with a low-stakes item just to have something on the agenda, open it up: anyone can bring an early-stage idea, a technical curiosity, or a "here's something I've been thinking about" for informal discussion. No funding decision required, no ADR required, just structured space for ideas that aren't ready for a formal pitch yet. It keeps the room's habit and rhythm intact, the same people, the same regular slot, the same expectation of showing up prepared to think carefully, without wasting the time when nothing formal needs review. It also creates a low-stakes on-ramp: an idea that draws interest in a salon session is the kind of thing ready to become a formal pitch at the next innovation tournament. Patterns that show up when a review board exists on the calendar but has stopped functioning as a forcing function. Reviews consistently approve with no pushback or requested changes No one can name a decision the board changed its mind about after seeing how it played out Board membership hasn't rotated in over a year Decisions aren't captured anywhere durable, no ADR, no written record, once the meeting ends Teams prepare a specific "board-ready" version of their architecture that differs from what's running in production

title: Board Reporting
description: A preview of the Technology Board Reporting Framework: what works reporting technology, security, and AI posture to a board.
body: Cadence & format The out-of-cycle escalation path Two clocks: internal escalation versus external disclosure Translating technical risk into business risk Investment & roadmap tied to outcomes Security & compliance posture Reporting on AI specifically Common mistakes, named directly Sample board deck How often the board hears from technology, and in what form, before a single word of content is decided. A consistent one-page technology summary attached to every board meeting, regardless of whether anything dramatic happened, plus a deeper technology review quarterly or semi-annually. Consistency builds the board's pattern recognition for what normal looks like, so they notice when something isn't. Technology only showing up on the agenda when something has gone wrong. This trains the board to associate a CTO presentation with bad news, which makes every appearance feel like a confession rather than a normal operating rhythm. The specific mechanism that makes a promise like "the quarterly report never contains a surprise" true, rather than aspirational. A pre-agreed threshold for what triggers a call to the board chair or committee lead outside the normal cadence, a confirmed material breach, a regulatory filing obligation, a decision that can't wait until the next scheduled meeting, defined before an incident happens rather than improvised during one. No defined threshold, which means every incident becomes a judgment call about whether it's board-worthy, made under pressure by whoever's closest to it.
