That's how a material issue ends up sitting until the next quarterly meeting for no reason other than nobody decided to escalate it sooner. For a public company, the out-of-cycle path above and the regulatory disclosure deadline are related but distinct, and conflating them creates legal exposure. The board should hear about a likely-material incident within roughly 24 hours, well ahead of any external deadline, so there's time to prepare a proper disclosure and align on the facts before anyone outside the company sees them. Under current SEC rules, a public company must disclose a cybersecurity incident determined to be material on Form 8-K within four business days of that materiality determination. The clock starts when materiality is decided rather than at discovery, which is why the internal escalation path needs to run well ahead of it rather than up against it. The single most common failure mode in board reporting: reporting the risk in the language it was diagnosed in rather than the language the board makes decisions in. "A vulnerability in our authentication system could allow unauthorized account access, affecting an estimated 40,000 customer accounts and carrying breach notification obligations in three states" states the business consequence first and the technical detail second, for anyone who wants it. "We have a CVSS 9.1 vulnerability in our OAuth implementation" is accurate and unusable by a board that isn't going to look up what CVSS 9.1 means mid-meeting. If a board member has to ask "what does that mean for us," the report failed before the discussion even starts. Connecting engineering spend and roadmap decisions to something the board governs: capital allocation and strategic risk. Framing a platform investment as "this reduces our customer onboarding time from six weeks to two, which our sales pipeline data shows is currently costing us an estimated 15 percent of qualified leads" ties the spend to a number the board already tracks. A roadmap slide organized by internal team names and sprint numbers. It's accurate to how the work is organized internally and meaningless to a board trying to understand what changes for the business and when. What a board needs to know here, distinct from an operational security review the CISO or security team runs separately. A small, stable set of metrics tracked over time: mean time to detect, mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities, percentage of the environment covered by current compliance certifications, third-party and vendor posture (percentage of vendors with a current SOC 2 or equivalent), and current cyber insurance coverage, with any material incidents since the last meeting and the incident response postmortem attached if one occurred. A wall of green checkmarks with no trend line, no incident history, and no sense of how the organization compares to industry peers. A board cannot distinguish "consistently secure" from "we've never measured this rigorously enough to find a problem" without a track record and an external reference point to compare against. An increasingly standard board expectation, and one most technology leaders haven't built a repeatable format for yet. A short standing section covering what AI systems are in production, what's spent on them, and what governance controls are in place, referencing the AI Governance Map's control layers directly rather than reinventing the language each quarter. Boards are increasingly asking about this whether or not it's offered, and forward-looking boards are starting to ask about emerging technology risk more broadly, post-quantum cryptography readiness, for example, is now a live board discussion topic at some companies. Treating an AI pilot as not board-relevant because it's "still experimental." If it touches customer data or a regulated decision, the board's risk oversight duty applies well before the system reaches full production, and finding out about it after an incident is worse than a modest early mention. Patterns that show up repeatedly enough to call out specifically rather than leave implicit in the sections above. Reporting activity (story points completed, deployments shipped) instead of outcomes (what changed for the business) Surprising the board with bad news in the meeting instead of a pre-brief to the chair or committee lead beforehand Treating every board update as a status report instead of occasionally using the time to ask the board for something specific: a decision, a resource, air cover for a hard tradeoff Before every board meeting, write one sentence per section: "what do I want the board to know, feel, or decide because of this." If a section doesn't have a clear answer to that, cut it or rework it. A board deck is a decision-support tool. Documentation belongs elsewhere. A seven-slide illustrative example applying every section above: at-a-glance metrics, business outcomes, security and AI posture, a risk heat map plus one risk translated into business terms, investment tied to outcomes, and a specific ask. Figures are synthetic; adapt the structure with your own numbers.

title: Build vs Buy
description: The criteria that decide a build-versus-buy debate, the differentiation test people misapply most often.
body: The criteria that decide it Score your own decision The differentiation test The maintenance question people skip The middle option nobody names: partner or extend Reversing the decision later Vendor risk beyond lock-in Signs the decision wasn't tested Most build-versus-buy debates get stuck arguing cost in isolation. Cost matters, but it's rarely the deciding factor once these have been answered. Question Leans build Leans buy Is this a differentiator? Yes, this is part of what customers pay for versus competitors No, it's necessary but customers don't choose you for it Does a mature vendor solution exist? No, or existing options are a poor fit for the requirement Yes, and it's been production-hardened by many other customers already Time to value You have runway to spend months getting it right You need it working in weeks rather than quarters Ongoing maintenance capacity You have, or are willing to build, a team that will own this indefinitely You don't want a permanent internal team dedicated to this domain Vendor lock-in risk if you buy Switching cost would be unacceptably high later Data portability and exit path are reasonable if the vendor relationship sours Score each criterion from the table above, 1 to 5, high meaning it leans build. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. The single most misapplied criterion, usually stretched to justify a decision already made for other reasons. A capability customers explicitly cite as why they chose you over an alternative, or one that materially changes your unit economics versus using a vendor. If you removed it, you'd lose deals or margin specifically because of its absence. "We want more control" or "the vendor's roadmap doesn't match ours exactly" are legitimate preferences. They aren't differentiation, and building an entire internal system to solve a preference is usually a worse trade than living with 90 percent fit from a vendor. Build decisions are evaluated on initial build cost far more often than on the ongoing cost of owning it for the next five years. Initial development time, initial infrastructure cost, time to first working version, the numbers that show up in a project proposal and are easy to estimate. Security patching indefinitely, keeping pace with a changing regulatory or integration landscape, the bus-factor risk when the one engineer who deeply understands it leaves, and the opportunity cost of the team's attention being split across build-and-maintain instead of focused on the differentiator. Build-versus-buy is usually presented as binary. A frequently better third option gets skipped. Buying a vendor platform for the undifferentiated 80 percent and building a thin, differentiated layer on top of it via the vendor's API or extension points, rather than building the whole stack from scratch or accepting 100 percent of the vendor's opinion. When the differentiation is narrow and specific (a particular workflow, a particular integration, a particular scoring model) rather than the whole domain. This is very often the right answer and gets dismissed early because the binary framing never surfaced it as an option. Build-versus-buy isn't necessarily a permanent choice. The sequencing of which comes first matters as much as the eventual answer. Start with a vendor to get to market fast. If the capability proves out as differentiation worth owning, build a deliberate replacement once you understand the requirements from having lived with the vendor's version, rather than guessing at them upfront. Building something in-house "to stay flexible" before you know whether it's a differentiator usually produces a worse version of what a mature vendor already built, at a cost that vendor already amortized across many customers instead of just you. The framework above asks whether you can leave a vendor. It's an incomplete question on its own. Lock-in asks "can I leave." It's worth also asking what happens if the vendor leaves you: acquisition risk, a pricing change once you're dependent, a wind-down of the specific product you rely on. See Vendor Evaluation for scoring this directly. A string of individually reasonable buy decisions, each cleared on its own lock-in and exit-cost merits, that quietly concentrate several important capabilities behind the same vendor. A single vendor's bad quarter becomes every one of those capabilities' bad quarter at once. Patterns that show up when a build-versus-buy call was made to justify a preference rather than worked through. Differentiation was asserted rather than tested against "would we lose deals or margin without this" No five-year total cost of ownership estimate exists for the build option, only the initial build cost The partner-or-extend middle option was never evaluated, only a binary build-or-buy framing No plan exists for reversing the decision later if the underlying assumption turns out wrong Vendor concentration across other decisions wasn't considered, only this one decision's lock-in risk in isolation

title: Business Case Calculator
description: A working NPV, IRR, and payback calculator for a multi-year technology investment, built on the same mechanics as the full business case workbook.
body: What the model produces Run the numbers What the pre-filled example represents Sensitivity: what happens if you're wrong Choosing a discount rate How business cases get gamed, and how to catch it Business case one-pager template Roll-up numbers from year-by-year cost and benefit inputs, the same structure as the full business case workbook: net present value, benefit-to-cost ratio, internal rate of return, and payback period. NPV: sum of discounted net cashflow across the analysis period Benefit-to-cost ratio: total benefits divided by total costs IRR: the discount rate at which NPV equals zero Payback period: when cumulative after-tax cashflow turns positive Verdict: a plain-language read on whether the case is strong, acceptable, or fragile NPV positive and B/C above roughly 1.5x reads as a strong case. NPV positive with B/C under 1.5x is worth funding, with the sensitivity checked before committing. These are illustrative reference points; your organization's bar depends on its cost of capital and risk appetite and should be set deliberately rather than borrowed from this page. NPV negative at base case doesn't automatically kill an initiative with strategic value that doesn't show up in the numbers, but it does mean the strategic argument has to carry the case explicitly instead of hiding behind an inflated financial one. Enter total costs and benefits per year. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. Defaults are pre-filled with a representative example so you can see it work before entering your own numbers. The default numbers loaded above are a representative modernization program. They are there to show the shape, so replace them with your own. Front-loaded implementation cost in Years 1 and 2, tapering to steady-state run cost by Year 3. Benefits ramp in behind it, typically 30 percent of steady-state value in Year 1, 70 percent in Year 2, full value from Year 3 onward, since adoption and realization lag the investment. A business case that assumes full benefit realization starting Year 1 is either describing a trivial change or overstating the case. Reviewers who've seen enough of these will discount an unramped benefit projection on sight. The most common gap between a business case that survives scrutiny and one that only looks solid under one set of assumptions. Run the same model at a pessimistic case, benefits 20 to 30 percent lower, costs 10 to 15 percent higher, before presenting the base case. If NPV still clears positive under the pessimistic scenario, the case is robust. If it only works at the base case, say so explicitly rather than letting the base case stand in for more confidence than the analysis supports. Presenting only the base case with no sensitivity shown. Either it was never tested, or it was tested, the pessimistic case failed, and it quietly got left out of the deck, which a CFO who's seen enough of these will assume by default even without being told. The single input most likely to be pulled from thin air, and the one most likely to quietly determine the verdict. The return the capital could earn elsewhere, the company's cost of capital if it tracks one, or a hurdle rate leadership has explicitly agreed represents good enough for a technology investment. 8 percent shows up often as an illustrative default for an established company, but it is only a placeholder. Your own cost of capital is company-specific and should replace it. A deliberately higher rate, 15 percent or more, is often used for early-stage or higher-risk bets specifically because the higher bar forces only the strongest cases through. Picking a lower discount rate because it makes more initiatives clear the bar, which quietly inflates the entire portfolio's apparent quality without anyone deciding to lower the standard. If the rate changes between two business cases with no stated reason, that's worth questioning before either number gets trusted. A handful of specific patterns account for most inflated cases. Worth knowing what to look for, whether reviewing someone else's case or checking your own. Double-counted benefits. The same cost saving claimed by two different initiatives' business cases, each one looking stronger on its own than the two deliver combined. A skipped ramp. Full benefit value assumed from Year 1, which is either describing a trivial change or quietly overstating the case, covered above. Costs that stop at go-live. The build cost is modeled carefully; the run cost the initiative adds afterward, ongoing licensing, additional on-call load, incremental support burden, never makes it into the model at all. A quietly adjusted discount rate. The rate shifts from the standard used elsewhere in the portfolio, with no stated reason, until the number clears the bar. Drop the NPV, IRR, benefit-to-cost, and payback numbers from the calculator above straight into this one-pager, alongside the problem statement, strategic rationale, and risks a pure financial model doesn't capture. Markdown for pasting into your own docs system, or a formatted Word doc.

title: Working with the CEO
body: What the CEO needs from a CTO Telling the CEO no A worked example Founder CEO versus professional CEO When technology should be invisible, and when it's the strategy Handling a CEO who's miscalibrated in either direction Building trust before you need it Escalation and cadence, stated explicitly Signs the relationship is unhealthy Four things a CEO can't get from anyone else on the team. Technical competence is assumed; none of these are about it. Need What it looks like What it isn't Translation Business strategy translated into its technology consequences, in language a non-technical executive can act on Technology strategy explained in a way that requires the CEO to already understand the technology Protection Technology risk surfaced while there's still time to do something about it Risk explained for the first time during the incident it caused Judgment A clear recommendation with the tradeoff stated plainly A menu of options with no point of view, leaving the decision entirely to someone without the context to make it well Predictability Commitments that hold, or an early, honest flag when they won't Optimistic timelines that quietly slip without anyone hearing about it until the deadline arrives The moment that defines the relationship more than any status update ever will. Arrive with the tradeoff already worked out alongside the refusal: "we can hit that date if we cut X, or hit full scope two weeks later, which do you want." A no with a stated alternative reads as judgment. A no with nothing behind it reads as an obstacle. A flat no delivered late, often after the CEO has already committed to the date externally, which turns a technical disagreement into a credibility problem for both people, and makes the next no much harder to deliver and to hear. What the mechanics above look like against a common scenario. The CEO wants to announce a launch date publicly at a conference six weeks out. The CTO's engineering estimate is ten weeks for the full feature set. Rather than a flat "we can't hit that," the CTO brings the tradeoff already worked out: a limited beta with three core features ships in six weeks, the full launch stays on the ten-week timeline. The CEO announces the beta at the conference instead of the full launch. Engineering hits the beta date. The full launch ships on the timeline that was true from the start. Nobody's public credibility gets damaged, because what got promised matched what was deliverable, and the CEO had a positive announcement to make either way. The same relationship, shaped very differently depending on who's in the role. Often has deep intuitive product and technical instincts even without a formal technical background, and personal identity tied closely to the company. Disagreements can feel personal in a way they don't with a professional CEO. Technical credibility gets earned through demonstrated judgment over time; the title alone buys none. Usually more process-oriented, expecting the same structured decision-rights model and reporting cadence used at previous companies. The relationship starts more transactional and earns trust faster through consistent, predictable execution rather than through personal rapport built up over years. Getting this posture wrong in either direction costs credibility. For most companies, most of the time, technology is an enabler. The goal is for the CEO to rarely have to think about it, and that quiet is a sign of health as long as it isn't masking a risk building underneath. When the technology is the competitive edge, what customers are buying is the technical capability, invisibility is the wrong posture. The CTO needs to be actively pushing technology into the CEO's strategic conversations instead of staying quietly out of them. Two opposite failure modes, requiring opposite corrections. Treats every technical detail as something worth personally weighing in on. Give them a small, explicit set of decisions that warrant their attention, rather than either blocking them out entirely or letting them relitigate implementation details that don't. Treat this as a translation failure rather than a values failure. Find the specific business metric technology investment moves, and lead every conversation with that number. Technical merit on its own gives the CEO nothing to evaluate it against. The high-stakes moments described above draw on a trust balance that has to be built somewhere else first. Regular, low-stakes contact, the weekly touchpoint described below, builds the trust that a high-stakes "telling the CEO no" moment later draws on. A CEO who's watched a CTO be right about smaller things repeatedly extends more benefit of the doubt when it matters most. The CTO only appears in the CEO's calendar when something's wrong, which means every interaction the CEO has with the CTO is colored by a problem, and trust never gets the chance to compound the way it does with regular, unremarkable contact. What should reach the CEO, and on what rhythm, shouldn't be reinvented every time something comes up. Escalate: a material change in risk, anything crossing a stated board-visibility threshold, and any commitment at risk of slipping, as early as it's known. Handle independently: implementation approach, internal architecture decisions, and day-to-day engineering management. A regular weekly touchpoint covers the practical items; a deeper monthly or quarterly conversation, tied to the broader operating cadence, covers strategy and portfolio; anything crossing an escalation threshold gets raised immediately rather than saved for the next scheduled meeting. Patterns that show up when the CEO-CTO relationship has drifted, regardless of how well either person would describe it individually. The CEO learns about a material technology risk from someone other than the CTO Every technology conversation with the CEO is either a routine status update or a crisis, nothing in between The CTO can't name the one or two business metrics the CEO tracks Disagreements get resolved by whoever escalates loudest rather than by a stated decision-rights model The CEO has stopped asking the CTO's opinion before making technology-adjacent decisions Most contact between the two only happens when something is already wrong

title: Cloud FinOps
description: Managing general infrastructure spend as a standing discipline rather than a quarterly panic when finance asks why the cloud bill jumped.
body: Phases: one building block of a larger framework Where cost hides Rightsizing and idle elimination Reserved capacity and commitment strategy Tagging, showback, and chargeback Governance without becoming a bottleneck FOCUS: a shared billing language across clouds Crawl, Walk, Run, applied practically Score your own FinOps maturity Signs cost governance isn't working Cloud FinOps workbook These are the FinOps Foundation's own Phases. The Foundation is the industry body (under the Linux Foundation) that maintains the full FinOps Framework and the FOCUS billing specification referenced throughout this page. The complete framework also includes Principles, Personas, Domains and Capabilities, and Scopes, and the Foundation's current definition centers on maximizing the business value of technology spend broadly rather than cloud alone. Cloud, SaaS, AI, data center, and licensing are all recognized Scopes; this page covers the cloud infrastructure scope, which is why AI cost modeling gets its own page rather than folding into this one. Phase Focus Typical activities Inform Visibility and allocation Tagging, showback, budgets, forecasting, benchmarking spend against peers Optimize Reducing waste and improving rates Rightsizing, reserved capacity and commitment discounts, workload rearchitecture for cost efficiency Operate Continuous governance Automated policies, anomaly detection, aligning engineering and finance around cost as a shared, ongoing metric The categories that consistently account for the largest share of avoidable spend, in roughly the order worth checking first. This is the Optimize phase in practice. Category What to look for Idle and oversized compute Instances provisioned for a peak load that rarely occurs, running at 10-15 percent utilization around the clock Non-production environments Dev, staging, and QA environments running 24/7 when they're only used during business hours Orphaned resources Volumes, snapshots, and load balancers left behind after the workload that used them was decommissioned Untagged spend Cost with no owning team attached, which nobody feels accountable for reducing because nobody's dashboard shows it Storage tiering Data sitting in a hot storage tier years after it stopped being accessed regularly Data egress Cross-region or cross-cloud transfer that could be avoided with different architecture, often invisible until the bill arrives The fastest money on the table, and the easiest to let slide once the first sweep is done. Automated shutdown for non-production environments outside business hours, utilization-based rightsizing recommendations reviewed monthly, and a default assumption that any resource untouched for 90 days gets flagged for a decommission decision rather than left alone indefinitely. Treating this as a one-time cleanup sprint instead of an ongoing practice. Six months after the sweep, utilization has drifted again and nobody's watching, because the tooling that found the savings the first time was never left running. Committing to reserved instances or savings plans locks in a discount and locks in a bet about future usage. Both halves matter. Commit only on the stable baseline, the usage level that's been consistent for at least six months, and use on-demand or short-term commitments for anything still growing or shrinking. Ladder commitment terms so not everything renews at once, which avoids a cliff where the whole discount structure needs renegotiating simultaneously. Overcommitting based on a growth projection that doesn't materialize, then paying for reserved capacity that sits unused, which is a worse outcome than paying on-demand rates for the same idle resource would have been. Cost visibility changes behavior. Cost invisibility guarantees nobody optimizes anything they can't see themselves accountable for. A mandatory tagging policy enforced at resource creation rather than applied retroactively by a cleanup script, with showback reporting that puts each team's spend in front of that team monthly. Chargeback, where teams' budgets are directly debited, is a stronger lever but works only once tagging discipline is already solid. Rolling out chargeback before tagging is reliable, which produces disputed, inaccurate bills that teams learn to ignore rather than a credible signal they act on. Trust in the numbers has to come before the numbers carry financial weight. The tension every cost program eventually hits: enough control to prevent waste, without so much that provisioning something new takes a week of approvals. Guardrails over gatekeeping: budget alerts that trigger automatically, instance-size policies enforced by infrastructure-as-code rather than a manual review, and approval requirements reserved for large or unusual spend rather than every new resource. Most cost control should be invisible to an engineer working within normal bounds. An approval queue that becomes the default path for routine provisioning, which teaches engineers to over-request once to avoid asking twice, producing the exact oversizing the governance process was meant to prevent. The FinOps Foundation's second major contribution beyond the phase model, and the reason cross-cloud cost comparison stopped being a manual exercise. Before FOCUS (the FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification), comparing a dollar of AWS spend to a dollar of Azure spend meant manually normalizing wildly different billing export formats, column names, and units. FOCUS is an open, vendor-neutral spec, now adopted by AWS, Microsoft, Google, and others, that puts every provider's billing data into the same shape. FOCUS standardizes the data format and leaves the underlying pricing and discount structures untouched. A normalized bill still requires the same rightsizing and commitment discipline covered above. FOCUS removes the translation tax from the reporting layer; the practice itself still has to happen. The FinOps Foundation's maturity model, stated concretely enough to assess against rather than claim. Crawl: tagging exists but is inconsistent, cost visibility is monthly and reactive, no forecasting. Walk: tagging enforced at creation, showback running, budgets set proactively, rightsizing is a recurring practice with an owner. Run: chargeback in place, unit economics tracked (cost per customer or transaction), anomaly detection automated, cost is a first-class input to architecture decisions rather than an afterthought. Treating maturity as a label to claim rather than a description of what's happening. An organization that calls itself "Run" but can't answer what a single team spent last month is Crawl with better branding. Six capability domains from the FinOps Foundation framework, scored 1 to 5. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. Not exhaustive, but the patterns that show up consistently when a cost program looks good on paper and isn't changing behavior. The last optimization effort was a one-time project with no recurring owner Untagged or misattributed spend is a growing percentage of the bill rather than shrinking Reserved capacity utilization is below 80 percent, meaning committed spend is going unused Non-production environments run around the clock with no automated schedule No one outside the finance or platform team can say what their own team's monthly cloud spend is The organization describes itself as FinOps "mature" but can't answer what a single team spent last month Six linked tabs: instructions, a rightsizing tracker, a reserved capacity break-even calculator, showback and chargeback allocation, the maturity assessment above made live, and a savings opportunity log. Every formula recalculates when you change an input.

title: Working with the CFO
body: What the CFO needs from a CTO Defending a number the CFO doesn't like When ROI framing doesn't fit, and saying so The budget conversation before the budget conversation Capitalization and accounting realities worth understanding Signs the relationship is unhealthy Different from what the CEO needs. The CEO wants judgment and a point of view; the CFO wants numbers that survive scrutiny. Need What it looks like What it isn't Predictable numbers A forecast that holds, or an early, honest flag the moment it won't A number that moves without warning and gets explained after the fact Defensible logic A stated method for how a figure was derived, so disagreement is about one assumption A number asserted with confidence but no visible derivation Honest framing ROI language where it fits, risk language where it doesn't ROI language forced onto every investment regardless of whether it applies No budget-meeting surprises Priorities shared before the formal cycle, so the CFO's first exposure isn't in a contentious room A ranked list revealed for the first time in front of other executives The moment that determines whether the relationship is adversarial or productive going forward. Show the derivation along with the conclusion. Walk through the specific assumption that, if changed, would change the number. Disagreement then becomes a conversation about one assumption, which is productive, instead of a vague sense that the number feels wrong, which goes nowhere. Presenting a number as settled fact with no visible derivation. Any pushback then becomes a credibility fight rather than a disagreement about a specific input, and credibility fights are much harder to walk back than assumption disagreements. Forcing every investment into ROI language is a common, well-intentioned mistake that costs credibility over time. Infrastructure consolidation, a specific automation replacing manual work, a feature with a modeled revenue impact. These reduce cleanly to a number, and the CFO relationship is healthiest when that number is presented as exactly what it is. Security investment, reliability investment, and technical debt remediation reduce risk and avoid future cost; they rarely produce a clean, defensible ROI figure. Forcing one produces a number nobody believes, which costs more credibility than justifying the investment on risk grounds instead. Where most CFO relationships go wrong: the timing of when the CFO first sees the numbers, more than the numbers themselves. Bring the CFO the pre-ranked capital allocation priorities before the formal budget cycle starts, in a one-on-one setting. The CFO should never see the logic behind technology priorities for the first time in a room with other executives present. The CFO's first exposure to how priorities were ranked happens live in the budget meeting itself, which makes every question feel adversarial even when it's just first contact with the reasoning. A CFO thinks in capex versus opex and amortization schedules. A CTO who understands the basics speaks the CFO's language instead of translating everything through an interpreter. Software development costs that qualify for capitalization under applicable accounting standards, versus costs that must be expensed immediately, materially change how a project's cost looks in a given quarter, independent of the project's actual value. Understanding this distinction, even at a high level, prevents a CTO from being caught off guard when a CFO cares more about the timing of a cost than its total, or pushes back on a schedule change that seems purely technical but carries a real capitalization consequence on the books. Patterns that show up when the CTO-CFO relationship has drifted into friction, regardless of how either person would describe it individually. Technology budget numbers get revised after the CFO has already committed them upward, more than once Every investment gets forced into ROI language regardless of whether it fits The CFO's first exposure to a priority ranking happens in a contentious budget meeting rather than before it The CTO can't explain, at a basic level, why a project's cost is phased the way it is on the books Disagreements about a number become personal rather than staying focused on a specific stated assumption

title: The CTO Operating System
body: The five tiers Areas of responsibility Time allocation by company stage Why cadence beats reactive prioritization Why allocation should shift over time Intended versus actual: where the time really goes The daily tier is smaller than it feels The quarterly reset is a reallocation decision The weekly tier: sync rather than status The annual tier, done properly A worked week, illustrative Signs the operating cadence has decayed Each tier exists to protect a different kind of work from being displaced by the others. The failure mode at each tier is different too. Tier What belongs here The failure mode Daily Active critical incidents, a risk that just became material, an executive blocker, a staffing emergency Anything that isn't time-sensitive creeps in, training the organization to escalate everything Weekly Engineering leadership sync, architecture and risk review, delivery health, recruiting, vendor issues Becomes a status-reporting ritual instead of a decision-making one Monthly Portfolio health, financials, security posture, reliability, people metrics Gets skipped under deadline pressure, exactly when it's most needed Quarterly Strategy reassessment, portfolio reallocation, board preparation, organizational health, technical debt review Treated as a report-out instead of a reallocation decision Annual Strategy reset, operating model, budget, org design, succession, architecture evolution, risk appetite Compressed into a single offsite instead of multi-week preparation The five tiers above answer when. This answers what, and where to go on this site for the full depth on each. Area What it covers Depth on this site Technology strategy & direction The three-horizon investment split, tradeoffs, competitive positioning Technology Strategy Architecture & technical standards Capability models, principles, review governance Enterprise Architecture, Architecture Principles, Architecture Review Board Team & organization Structure, hiring, leveling, culture Org Design, Technical Hiring & Leveling, Engineering Culture Capital allocation & budget Portfolio-level investment decisions and the standing budget process Technology Capital Allocation, Running the Technology Budget Risk & security Stated risk appetite, security program, resilience Technology Risk Appetite, Security Program, Disaster Recovery Executive & board relationships The relationships that determine whether anything above gets funded or heard Working with the CEO, Working with the CFO, Board Reporting Delivery oversight Whether the organization is shipping, reliably, and knows it Engineering Metrics, Platform Engineering, Incident Response Hands-on technical work Direct coding, architecture deep-dives, code review No dedicated page; this is the category with the steepest decline as the organization scales, covered in the allocation table below M&A & diligence Applies only during an active transaction; there is no steady-state allocation Technology Diligence, Technology M&A Integration Illustrative rather than measured. The direction of the shift is the point, and no single number is precise; treat these as a starting frame to check your own calendar against rather than a target to hit exactly. Area Early-stage (under 50 eng) Scale-stage (50-500 eng) Enterprise (500+ eng) Technology strategy & direction 8% 15% 20% Architecture & technical standards 12% 15% 10% Team & organization 20% 20% 15% Capital allocation & budget 3% 8% 13% Risk & security 2% 7% 8% Executive & board relationships 10% 15% 22% Delivery oversight 15% 12% 10% Hands-on technical work 30% 8% 2% M&A and diligence isn't in the table because it isn't a steady-state allocation; it spikes heavily during an active transaction regardless of stage and returns to near-zero afterward. The alternative to a stated cadence is an implicit one where whoever's loudest wins. Separates urgent from important by giving each its own guaranteed slot, so a crisis doesn't consume the time that should go to the quarterly reallocation decision, and a quarterly review doesn't get treated with an urgency it doesn't warrant. Everything competes for attention at the same priority, and daily fires win every time by default. Long-horizon work, technical debt, succession planning, architecture evolution, never gets protected time because nothing forces it onto the calendar. The table above is one trajectory rather than three unrelated snapshots, and the shift itself has to be managed deliberately. Deliberately renegotiating your own time allocation at each scaling milestone (a new engineering VP hired, an architecture function stood up, a CFO relationship established), rather than letting the shift happen passively or resisting it out of habit. A CTO who keeps writing code and reviewing every pull request well past the point the org has outgrown that involvement becomes the bottleneck they used to prevent. A CTO who delegates architecture and technical judgment before the org has anyone ready to hold it leaves a capability gap disguised as "scaling the team." Most CTOs, asked to describe their allocation, would sketch something close to the table above. Their calendar usually disagrees. An audited calendar usually shows meetings and reactive interruptions consuming twenty to thirty percentage points more than intended, almost always stolen from technology strategy and hands-on deep work, the two categories with no urgent deadline forcing their own defense. The Thursday deep-work block described later on this page is the mechanism that defends strategy time from being silently eaten by whatever's urgent that particular week. Audit the calendar quarterly against the intended allocation; a gut sense of how the time is going is usually wrong in the same direction. Daily access to the CTO is available, which is exactly why the daily tier is the one most prone to creep. Only what can't wait: an active Sev1 or Sev2, a risk that just crossed a material threshold, an executive blocker stopping other work, a staffing emergency. If it could wait a week without cost, it isn't a daily item. Status updates, routine decisions, and anything convenient get pulled into daily attention simply because the CTO is reachable. Once this starts, the daily tier stops protecting anything and becomes the default channel for everything. The tier most likely to exist on the calendar and produce nothing. A change: capital moved between horizons, a strategic assumption revisited and possibly overturned, an initiative killed. If nothing changed, the review didn't do its job, regardless of how thorough the discussion was. A calendar ritual summarizing the quarter that already happened, with no mechanism forcing a reallocation decision. The portfolio mix persists by inertia rather than by choice, and everyone leaves the room having confirmed what they already believed. The tier that runs most often and is therefore most at risk of becoming ritual rather than function. The weekly sync exists to make decisions that can't wait for the monthly review but don't rise to daily urgency: a hiring tradeoff, a scope cut, a risk needing more than one function's input. Attendees arrive having already read written updates, so the room's time goes to discussion and decisions rather than readout. A round-robin status update where each function reports what it already reported in writing, consuming an hour that produces no decision. The decisions then happen in a separate, smaller, unscheduled conversation right after the official meeting ends, which quietly tells everyone where the work happens. The tier most often compressed, and the one where compression costs the most. Weeks of groundwork before the offsite itself: the capital allocation review already run, the succession heatmap already updated, input already gathered from the people who'll be in the room. The offsite is for decisions and alignment; nobody should be seeing the material for the first time there. A two-day offsite where strategy, budget, and org design all get worked out live in the room for the first time, producing decisions made on the spot that get quietly revisited and often reversed in the following weeks, once people have had time to think about material they were seeing for the first time under pressure. What the tiers look like assembled into one calendar, for a CTO at roughly a 150-engineer organization. Day What's on it Monday Weekly engineering leadership sync (60 min), written updates read in advance, agenda limited to decisions needed this week Tuesday 1:1s with direct reports, protected time for a Horizon 3 review if one is scheduled that month Wednesday Architecture Review Board slot (biweekly), CFO or CEO touchpoint if one is due this week Thursday Deep work block, no standing meetings, reserved for whatever the quarterly or annual tier currently needs preparation time for Friday Monthly portfolio and financial review (when due), otherwise a lighter day absorbing whatever the week's daily-tier items turned out to be The specific days don't matter. What matters is that Thursday's block exists at all: without a protected slot for the work that isn't urgent this week, it never happens, because something urgent is always available to fill the time instead. The cadence can exist on a calendar and still not be functioning. These patterns show up when it's decayed into performance rather than practice. Daily conversations routinely include topics that could have waited a week The monthly portfolio or financial review has been skipped or shortened for three or more consecutive months Quarterly reviews haven't produced a capital reallocation in over a year No one outside the CTO could describe what happens at each cadence tier Annual strategy work gets compressed into a single offsite with little preparation beforehand The weekly sync consistently produces no decisions, and the decisions happen in a separate, unscheduled conversation afterward The calendar hasn't been audited against an intended time allocation in over a year, or ever Hands-on technical work hasn't declined as a share of time despite the organization scaling well past the stage where that made sense

title: CTO Leadership & Succession
body: The questions a succession plan has to answer The bus-factor question, applied to leadership Building the bench deliberately The leadership succession heatmap The heatmap, worked Emergency versus planned succession are different playbooks What the board needs to know, and when Signs succession is assumed rather than planned If any of these has no answer, that is the finding, and it matters more than the document. Who can run engineering if the CTO is out for ninety days? Who can represent technology to the board? Who can run a major incident from start to finish? Who owns architecture, in practice rather than by title? Who is willing to challenge the CTO's thinking, and does the CTO listen to them? Where is institutional knowledge concentrated, and what happens to it if that person leaves? The same discipline already applied to code ownership, extended to people in leadership roles. Name the specific individuals whose departure would create a multi-month gap in a specific capability. A generic sense that "the team is strong" names nobody. Bus-factor analysis works the same way for leadership as it does for a codebase: identify where there's exactly one person who can do something critical. Assuming seniority or title implies succession readiness. A VP title doesn't mean that person could credibly represent technology to the board tomorrow if asked to do it without warning. A bench that exists by accident usually turns out not to exist at all when it's tested. Give a successor candidate exposure before they need it: board attendance, incident command rotation, ownership of an architecture review. The first time someone does something this consequential shouldn't be during an emergency. Protecting a strong deputy from visibility because delegating feels slower than doing it yourself in the moment, which guarantees the organization has no bench when it's tested. A small artifact that makes the state of succession visible instead of assumed. For each critical leadership function, name the current owner, the identified successor, and their readiness: ready now, six to twelve months out, or not yet started. A "none identified" in several rows is the finding the exercise exists to surface. It does not mean the document was filled out incorrectly. What a filled-in version looks like, including the gaps most organizations would rather not write down. Function Current owner Identified successor Readiness Represent technology to the board CTO VP Engineering 6 to 12 months out Run engineering day-to-day CTO Director of Engineering Ready now Own architecture decisions Principal Architect None identified Not started Run a major incident end to end Head of SRE Senior SRE Lead Ready now Represent technology in an M&A conversation CTO None identified Not started The two "none identified" rows are the output of this exercise. An organization that fills every row in green either has an exceptional bench or went easy on itself; both are worth double-checking. Confusing the two produces a plan that works for neither scenario. The interim owner named on the heatmap steps in immediately. Communication goes out within 24 to 48 hours, framed around continuity. The board is looped in the same day. The goal is stability. Naming a permanent replacement can wait weeks; the stability signal can't. Use the notice period deliberately. The successor takes on visible responsibility gradually across the transition window rather than all at once on the last day. The departing CTO makes introductions, to the board, key customers, key vendors, personally, rather than leaving the successor to build those relationships cold after the fact. Enough to avoid surprise. The detailed heatmap stays internal. The board should know a succession plan exists and who the interim contact would be, discussed at least annually as part of a broader risk conversation, the same cadence as the risk appetite review, rather than sprung on them during a departure. The board's first exposure to "who runs technology if the CTO leaves" is the day the CTO leaves, which is exactly the worst moment to be building consensus on an interim leader while also managing the departure itself. Patterns that show up when succession planning exists as an idea but not as a tested plan. No one has been identified who could run engineering for ninety days without the CTO The people who could represent technology to the board have never done it Succession candidates have title and tenure but no exposure to the responsibilities they'd inherit The heatmap, if it exists, hasn't been updated since the last reorg A single individual's departure would create a gap the organization has no plan for The board has never heard the succession plan discussed outside of a departure

title: Data Governance & Privacy
body: Which regulation applies, and when Data classification as the foundation Subject access and deletion requests, operationally A worked example: a request end to end Ownership versus stewardship Privacy by design rather than privacy as a review gate Breach notification, the mechanics Cross-border data transfer, briefly Governance red flags A starting map rather than a legal determination. Applicability depends on where customers are located, what data is collected, and industry-specific rules; confirm with counsel. Framework Triggers when Core obligation GDPR Processing personal data of individuals in the EU/EEA, regardless of where the company is based Lawful basis for processing, subject access and deletion rights, breach notification within 72 hours CCPA / CPRA Processing personal data of California residents above certain revenue or volume thresholds Disclosure of data collected, opt-out of sale/sharing, deletion rights HIPAA Handling protected health information as a covered entity or business associate Safeguards on PHI, breach notification, business associate agreements with vendors Sector and state-specific Financial services, children's data, and a growing list of individual state privacy laws Varies; often layered on top of the frameworks above rather than replacing them Every governance obligation downstream depends on first knowing what data exists and how sensitive it is. A classification scheme with a small number of clear tiers, public, internal, confidential, restricted or regulated, applied at the point data is created or collected rather than retrofitted later through an audit. Every system holding data above the lowest tier has a named owner accountable for it. A classification policy that exists on paper but was never applied to the systems in production, so nobody can answer a basic question like "where does our customer PII live" without a multi-week investigation. The rights GDPR and similar frameworks grant individuals are only real if the organization can fulfill them within the required window. A documented, at least partially automated process for locating and exporting or deleting an individual's data across every system that holds it, tested against a live request rather than assumed to work. A tracked SLA against the regulatory deadline, with an owner accountable for meeting it. Fulfillment handled manually by whichever engineer is available, searching system by system with no authoritative list of where personal data lives, which routinely blows past the regulatory response window on anything beyond the simplest request. What the practice above looks like against an incoming request, including where it commonly breaks. A request arrives through a web form and gets logged against the SLA clock immediately. The response process checks it against the data inventory: CRM, product database, support ticketing, and email marketing tool are all on the list, get queried, and the results get compiled into a portable export within the regulatory window. Where it commonly breaks: the analytics warehouse isn't on the inventory, because nobody classified it as holding personal data even though it has user IDs joinable back to an identity through the product database. The request gets marked complete while a meaningful chunk of what the organization holds on that person was never touched. This is why the inventory in section 1 has to be built by mapping data flows rather than by asking each team what they think they hold. Two different roles that get conflated, and the conflation is where accountability gaps live. A data owner is accountable for the business decisions around a dataset, retention, access policy, whether it should exist at all. A data steward implements those decisions day to day, quality checks, access provisioning, pipeline maintenance. The same person can hold both roles, but the accountability should be explicit either way. Data that's used operationally by several teams but formally owned by none of them, so retention and access decisions never get made deliberately, they just accumulate as whatever the default happened to be. Where privacy consideration enters the development process changes how much friction it creates and how much risk it catches. A lightweight privacy impact assessment built into the design phase for any feature touching personal data, before implementation starts, so decisions about what to collect and how long to keep it are made deliberately rather than defaulted to "collect everything, figure out retention later." Privacy review as a gate right before launch, which arrives too late to change the data model, so findings either get overridden under deadline pressure or become expensive retrofits after the feature is already live and being used. The 72-hour clock most people have heard of, and the specific way organizations usually miss it despite meaning to comply. The 72-hour window starts when the organization becomes aware of a breach, well before it's fully understood. A preliminary notification with known facts, followed by updates as the investigation progresses, is compliant. Waiting for a complete picture before notifying anyone is a violation. Treating the deadline as something to hit only once the full scope is understood, which routinely blows past 72 hours since an investigation almost always takes longer than that, when a partial, updated notification would have been compliant from day one. A specific, common gap that surfaces during customer security reviews more often than during an internal audit. Standard Contractual Clauses or an equivalent mechanism for transferring EU personal data outside the EEA, documented per vendor. A vendor's general terms of service do not cover it by default. Discovering during a customer security questionnaire that data has been flowing to a vendor or a region with no transfer mechanism in place, sometimes for years, because nobody mapped where data goes once it leaves the primary system. Patterns that show up when data governance exists as policy and stops there. No single, current inventory of where personal or regulated data lives across the estate Subject access or deletion requests handled manually with no tracked SLA against the regulatory deadline Data retained indefinitely by default because no one made an active decision to delete it Third-party vendors processing personal data with no data processing agreement or business associate agreement on file Privacy consideration enters the process only as a pre-launch review, never during design No documented transfer mechanism exists for personal data moving to vendors or regions outside its origin

title: Data Strategy
body: Warehouse, lakehouse, or mesh Data as a product rather than a project The operating model: centralized versus federated data teams Data literacy and self-service for everyone beyond engineering The golden record problem Metadata, catalog, and lineage Data quality as an AI prerequisite Real-time versus batch, as a strategic decision Build versus buy for the data stack Migrating between patterns without a rewrite Data contracts, made concrete Data as a product to external customers Signs the data strategy isn't working The architectural choice most data strategy conversations start with. It is one of eleven topics on this page, and far from the whole strategy. Definitions first, then the tradeoff. Pattern What it is Fits when Struggles when Data warehouse A central repository holding structured, pre-cleaned data, modeled and indexed for fast BI and reporting queries. Structured, well-understood reporting needs, a single team can reasonably own data quality centrally Data sources are highly heterogeneous or domain ownership needs to be distributed Data lakehouse Cheap, flexible storage for raw data in any format, with a warehouse-style query and schema layer built on top of it. Mixed structured and unstructured data, need for both BI and ML workloads on the same underlying data Organizational discipline around schema and quality is weak; a lakehouse without governance becomes a swamp fast Data mesh A decentralized operating model: each business domain owns, publishes, and is accountable for its own data as a product, instead of one central team owning all of it. Large organization with independent domains, each with the capacity to own their own data product Applied to an organization too small to staff domain-level data ownership; the coordination overhead exceeds the benefit The mindset shift underneath data mesh, applicable even in organizations not adopting the full mesh architecture. A data pipeline gets built once to answer a specific question, then quietly rots as the source system changes underneath it, with no owner responsible for noticing or fixing the drift until a report breaks and someone escalates. A dataset has a named owner, a defined quality bar, a consumer-facing contract (schema, freshness, meaning of each field), and a deprecation process, the same discipline applied to an internal API, applied to data instead. The organizational question underneath data mesh. Mesh describes how data is structured and owned technically; this is who's staffed, and where they report. One team owns data infrastructure, pipelines, and quality end to end across the whole company. Consistent standards and a single point of accountability, but becomes a bottleneck as the number of data-consuming teams grows past what one team can service responsively. Data engineers embedded within each domain team, closer to the business context and faster to respond to that domain's needs. Standards and quality drift apart across domains without a strong central platform layer underneath providing shared tooling and governance. Most data strategies are written for the people building the pipelines. This is about everyone else. A defined, curated set of self-service tools and pre-modeled datasets a non-technical analyst can query directly with guardrails, paired with training investment. A BI tool license handed out on its own is access, and access alone is not self-service. Self-service rolled out as tool access alone, which produces a proliferation of inconsistent, ungoverned dashboards each answering the same business question slightly differently, worse for decision-making than the centralized bottleneck it was meant to fix. Master data management's central challenge: the same real-world entity represented differently across systems, with no single system holding the authoritative version. Customer data alone commonly lives in a CRM, a billing system, a support tool, and a product database, each with its own ID, its own update cadence, and its own partial view. Picking one as automatically authoritative is rarely right for every field. A defined source-of-truth mapping at the field level rather than the entity level: billing system is authoritative for payment status, CRM is authoritative for account ownership, product database is authoritative for usage data. Merge logic follows the mapping rather than picking one system to trust for everything. The layer that answers "what data do we have, what does it mean, and what breaks if I change it," consistently the weakest layer in organizations that otherwise have their data strategy in order. A catalog and lineage graph don't show up in a quarterly roadmap the way a new pipeline or dashboard does, and the pain of not having them is diffuse: a slow, five-hop manual trace when a report breaks, a schema change shipped without knowing which six downstream jobs depend on it, an analyst who can't tell if a dataset is still owned or safe to trust. None of that shows up as a single dramatic incident, so it stays permanently below the cutline. A catalog makes data discoverable and answers who owns it and whether it's still trustworthy. Lineage traces the path from source system to final dashboard or model, so a schema change or a broken pipeline can be traced to every downstream consumer in minutes instead of hours of tribal-knowledge archaeology. Both compound directly into the migration work further down this page (you can't safely run old and new in parallel if you don't know what depends on what) and into the AI grounding problem below (an agent that can't see schema, lineage, and ownership will guess). Why this page and the AI Governance Map's data foundation layer are describing the same underlying problem from two different altitudes. An AI system retrieving from or trained on poor-quality, poorly owned data inherits every one of that data's problems, at scale and with less visibility into the failure than a human analyst working the same data manually would have had. Data quality and ownership work is the same foundational investment whether or not AI is on the roadmap, so it doesn't need to be framed as a prerequisite project to finish first. An organization with strong data product discipline has most of what AI governance's Layer 1 requires already in place. An implementation detail on the surface, and an economic decision underneath, the same shape as the argument on Reliability as an Economic Decision, applied to data freshness instead of system uptime. Fraud detection, live personalization, operational alerting, use cases where the value of the insight decays to near-zero within minutes or seconds, justifying real-time infrastructure's higher operational complexity and cost. Building real-time streaming infrastructure for a report that gets looked at once a week. The freshness nobody needed doesn't add value; it just adds an ongoing operational tax the same way an unneeded ninth of availability does. See Build vs Buy for the general framework. Data tooling is one of the clearest places it applies. ETL and ELT tooling, data catalogs, and BI platforms are mature, competitive markets. Building these in-house rarely produces a competitive advantage and usually recreates a worse version of what's commercially available. A novel data product that is itself the company's competitive differentiation. The infrastructure underneath it still gets bought. The same differentiation test from Build vs Buy applies directly: would the company lose deals or margin without owning this specifically. Almost no organization starts on the right pattern and stays there forever. How the migration happens matters as much as which pattern is the eventual target. Run the new pattern alongside the old one for specific domains first, proving value on a bounded scope before cutting anything over globally. The same strangler-fig discipline covered on Legacy Modernization Execution applies directly here: incremental migration instead of a single rip-and-replace event. Announcing a full data platform migration as a single multi-quarter program with no intermediate value delivered along the way. Executive patience for a program with no visible output runs out well before a data platform migration typically finishes. "Data contract" gets used loosely. A contract that doesn't specify these things isn't one. The schema, a freshness commitment (how current the data is guaranteed to be), the meaning of each field in plain language, and a deprecation policy for breaking changes, published somewhere consumers can find and reference it rather than carried in a single engineer's memory. A schema definition with no freshness commitment and no deprecation process. Consumers build against it anyway, because it's the only documentation available, and get broken silently the first time the upstream schema changes without warning. A question worth asking explicitly, even for organizations that will answer no. For some organizations, the data itself, aggregated, anonymized, or offered directly, is a monetization opportunity distinct from its internal analytical use. This isn't relevant to every company, but it's worth asking deliberately: does this organization sit on data that would be valuable to someone else, and if so, is productizing it worth the privacy, security, and packaging investment that would require. The answer for most companies is no, but it should be a considered no rather than a question nobody asked. Patterns that show up when a data strategy exists on a slide but isn't shaping how data gets built and maintained. No dataset has a named owner accountable for its quality A migration between patterns has stalled in an expensive middle state, both old and new running indefinitely with no plan to finish Data contracts, where they exist, specify a schema but no freshness or deprecation commitment The same real-world entity holds conflicting values across systems with no field-level source-of-truth mapping to resolve it AI initiatives are blocked by data quality issues that were already flagged as a data strategy risk before the AI initiative started Self-service access was granted with no curation or training, producing multiple dashboards that answer the same question differently Real-time infrastructure exists for a use case nobody has ever needed the data faster than daily for The centralized-versus-federated data team question was never decided deliberately, it just happened by accident of hiring

title: Decision ArchitectureSix stages from strategy to measurement, with the loop back to strategy
description: The actual shape underneath the 52 pages: six interconnected domains, a feedback loop, and a foundational layer that doesn't fit a sequence.
body: The shape, drawn What are we trying to do How decisions get made, and by whom What gets built, and how it's structured Where the constraints and control mechanisms live Where it happens, day to day Whether any of it worked Making one decision well What doesn't fit the sequence, and why forcing it would mislead Six interconnected domains below: which page applies to which part of running the function, from setting direction to measuring whether it worked. PrOACT: the process for making one decision well, run inside whichever of the six domains that decision currently sits in. Foundational: standing habits of mind, evaluating evidence, seeing interconnection, managing key relationships, active regardless of domain or decision. Six stages in sequence, one loop, one separation. Every page on this site sits in one of the six boxes, in the loop, or in the two bands underneath. The green loop is Deming's plan-do-check-act applied to the whole function: measurement is the input to the next strategy rather than the end of the sequence. The dashed bracket is COBIT's separation of governing from managing, which is why operating model and governance are different stages. Direction and priority, before anything gets built or governed. Turning direction into a functioning system: roles, rhythms, decision rights. The technical shape: systems, platforms, the application estate. The specific decisions worth constraining and why. Centralization for its own sake is a different thing. Delivery, incidents, people, the work itself once direction and constraints are set. The evidence that feeds back into Strategy, closing the loop rather than ending it. Hammond, Keeney, and Raiffa's PrOACT framework (Smart Choices, 1999, building on Howard Raiffa's earlier decision analysis work) provides a structured sequence for making a decision well, run inside whichever of the six domains the decision currently sits in. PrOACT step What it looks like Where it lives here Frame the Problem State what's being decided, and what's explicitly out of scope Strategy, Technology Strategy Objectives State what you're optimizing for before you look at options, so the options don't retroactively define the goal Strategy, Business Case Calculator Alternatives Options that could each win, rather than the one you already prefer plus a straw man Governance, ADRs & Roadmapping Consequences Confidence-graded evidence for what each alternative produces Foundational, Epistemology & Research Methods Tradeoffs Explicit scoring against the same criteria, so the tradeoff is visible instead of hidden inside a gut call Strategy, Vendor Evaluation Choose A named, accountable owner makes the call Operating Model, Technology Decision Rights Implement and monitor Ship it, then check whether it produced what the objectives step said it should Execution and Measurement, Engineering Metrics Six pages that are never a step you pass through once. They sit underneath every domain or run continuously alongside all of them.

title: Disaster Recovery & Business Continuity
body: RTO and RPO, defined by tier Setting RTO and RPO Backup testing discipline Tabletop exercises Multi-region versus single-region, costed Answering the board question Is the faster recovery time worth its cost? Communicating DR investment as insurance DR red flags Recovery Time Objective is how long the business can tolerate a system being down. Recovery Point Objective is how much data loss is acceptable. Both should be set by business impact rather than by what's technically easy. Tier Example systems Typical RTO Typical RPO Tier 1: Revenue-critical Payment processing, core transaction systems, customer-facing platform Minutes to under 1 hour Near-zero, seconds to minutes Tier 2: Operationally important Internal tools, reporting, secondary customer channels 4 to 24 hours Minutes to hours Tier 3: Deferred impact Archival systems, non-urgent internal tools Days Up to 24 hours The most common DR failure is a target that was never realistic in the first place; the bad recovery only exposes it. Ask the business owner what happens at 1 hour, 4 hours, and 24 hours of downtime for each system, in dollars or customer impact, then set the target from that answer. The target should hurt to miss; if missing it wouldn't matter, the system is probably a lower tier than it's currently classified. An RTO of 4 hours written into a policy document, never tested, while the infrastructure would take 2 days to recover. The number on paper and the number that's true are different, and nobody finds out which one is real until a disaster. A backup that has never been restored is a hypothesis. Scheduled, automated restore tests, rather than manual ones someone remembers to run occasionally, with the restore time measured and compared against the stated RTO every time. A backup that restores successfully but takes 3x longer than the RTO promises is a finding. Backups that run successfully and are never restored until the day they're needed, at which point corruption, missing dependencies, or forgotten configuration steps turn a routine recovery into an extended outage. Rehearsing the decision-making as well as the technical recovery steps. A scheduled exercise, at least annually for Tier 1 systems, that walks a realistic scenario end to end: who declares the disaster, who has authority to fail over, how customers get notified, and how the team knows recovery is complete rather than just visually normal again. A DR plan that's technically sound but has never been rehearsed by the humans who'd execute it, so the event itself surfaces confusion about authority and sequencing that the document assumed away. Multi-region resilience is expensive, and the expense is often invisible until someone prices it out. Cost the multi-region architecture (data replication, cross-region networking, the operational overhead of maintaining two live environments) against the quantified cost of the downtime it prevents. For revenue-critical systems, this usually clears the bar. For everything else, it often doesn't. Multi-region architecture applied uniformly across the whole estate because it feels like the responsible default, without anyone pricing whether the systems getting that treatment warrant it. "What's our recovery time if we lose a region" is a standard board question. The credible answer is specific rather than reassuring. A credible answer names the tier, states the tested RTO with the date it was last verified, and states which systems don't yet meet target. "We're covered" without those specifics is the answer of someone who hasn't tested it recently, and board members who've heard that answer before know the difference. The same cost-benefit logic as Reliability as an Economic Decision, applied to recovery speed instead of uptime. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. See Working with the CFO for the general argument about when ROI framing doesn't fit. DR spend is one of the clearest examples. Frame DR investment the way an insurance purchase gets framed: an expected-value calculation across many possible years rather than a promised return in any single year. The probability input in the calculator above is an estimate, and saying so out loud is more credible than pretending it is precise. Presenting a DR business case with the same confident ROI language used for a revenue-generating feature, which invites exactly the wrong question, "did we get that return this year," when the true answer is that a well-run DR program often means the disaster didn't happen to test it. Patterns that show up consistently when a disaster recovery program looks complete on paper and isn't. RTO and RPO targets exist in a document but have never been tested against measured recovery time The last full-scale restore test or tabletop exercise was more than a year ago, or has never happened Recovery depends on a single person's institutional knowledge rather than a documented, rehearsed runbook Backup and primary infrastructure share a failure domain, same region, same provider account, same network path, undermining the recovery they're meant to enable Tier classification hasn't been revisited since the systems it covers changed significantly DR investment gets pitched with certain-return ROI language rather than framed as insurance against a probabilistic event

title: EA Maturity Assessment
body: What this assessment is for The six dimensions Score your own function Running it as a full assessment Diagnostic patterns the calculator flags Reading one score pattern Turning the result into a twelve-month roadmap Scoring on intent Produces two things and nothing more: a defensible baseline across six dimensions, and a starting position for a twelve-month improvement plan. It doesn't produce a grade. A new EA leader takes over the function An organization is deciding whether to invest in EA at all An established function has plateaued and needs a structured look at why 1, Absent: no recognizable version exists 2, Emerging: exists in pockets, driven by specific individuals, unreliable beyond them 3, Defined: named, documented, applied consistently in most cases 4, Managed: measured, reviewed, improves in response to data 5, Optimized: integrated into business decision-making with evidence of enterprise-wide impact Each answers a different question about the function. A function can be strong in one and weak in another; that unevenness is the useful signal, and averaging it away loses it. Dimension What it asks Strategy Alignment Does EA's work connect to the strategy the enterprise is pursuing? The dimension most commonly rated optimistically. Governance Are architectural decisions made through a process that scales, with exceptions tracked and reviews credible to delivery teams? Domain Coverage Does the function cover the domains EA should cover, or is it a strong application-architecture function playing above its weight class? Delivery Integration Does EA produce better decisions in delivery, or operate as a parallel track delivery works around? Talent & Operating Model Is the function organized to be sustainable: roles, succession, sponsor relationships, demand management? Artifacts & Tooling Does the function maintain what it produces, at a cost proportionate to the value? Scored last and carefully; the easiest dimension to over-invest in. Rate each dimension 1 to 5. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. For a full assessment, score independently across 2 to 4 scorers before reconciling, per the facilitator guidance below; this calculator is for a single scorer's pass. This page's calculator is a single-scorer pass. A full assessment is deliberately multi-evaluator, same principle as the vendor scorecard, for the same reason. The EA leader scores, plus two to four others selected for angle of view rather than seniority: a senior delivery leader, a business sponsor who consumes EA output, an outside solution architect, optionally a prior EA leader. Avoid scorers who have a position to defend. Each scorer completes the assessment independently, same briefing, same scale, no discussion, forty-five minutes. Then a ninety-minute session, dimension by dimension: where scores diverge by more than one point, discuss it. The discussion is the data, and persistent divergence is itself a finding worth preserving rather than averaging away. The average hides the finding. These are the score shapes that recur, what each usually means, and what to do about it before building a roadmap. Pattern What it usually means First move Artifacts & Tooling high, Delivery Integration low A documentation function. The models are beautiful and delivery teams do not consult them Stop producing artifacts for a quarter; embed architects in the two most important delivery streams and measure whether decisions change Strategy Alignment high, everything else low The EA leader is trusted by executives and the function has no machinery beneath that trust Governance first: a lightweight review path with a written exception process, so the trust converts into decisions that stick Governance high, Delivery Integration low A gate. Reviews happen, delivery teams route around them, and the exception log is where the architecture that ships gets decided Move review earlier and make it evidence-based; see Architecture Review Board Domain Coverage low, all else moderate A strong application architecture group called EA. Data, security, and business architecture are uncovered Name the uncovered domains explicitly and decide whether to staff them, partner for them, or state that they are out of scope Talent & Operating Model at 1 or 2 with anything at 4 Key-person risk. The function's maturity is one resignation away from a 2 Succession and demand management before any further capability investment Uniform 3s Either a balanced, mid-maturity function or a single scorer who did not want to commit. The multi-scorer process tells you which Run the reconciliation session before drawing any conclusion The score that most often surprises the EA leader who runs it on their own function.
