Govern provides the organizational context and direction for the other five, added in CSF 2.0 because a technically mature program with no executive-level ownership or risk strategy is a common gap. Function Level 1: Ad hoc Level 3: Defined Level 5: Optimized Govern No documented cybersecurity risk strategy at the leadership level; security reports up as a technical status update rather than a business risk Named executive accountability, a documented risk management strategy, and defined reporting cadence to leadership or the board Cybersecurity risk is a standing item in enterprise risk management, with roles, policy, and supply chain risk expectations reviewed on a defined schedule rather than only after an incident forces it Identify No current asset inventory; risk assessment happens reactively after an incident Documented asset inventory, periodic risk assessments on a defined schedule Continuous, automated asset discovery feeding a live risk register tied to business impact Protect Access controls inconsistent across systems; no formal least-privilege policy Documented access control policy, applied through a defined onboarding and offboarding process Least-privilege enforced automatically, access reviewed continuously rather than only at audit time Detect Reliant on external reports or customer complaints to learn about a problem Centralized logging and defined alerting rules for known threat patterns Behavioral anomaly detection running alongside signature-based rules, catching a wider range of patterns than either alone, though no detection approach guarantees catching a novel attack Respond No defined incident process; response improvised each time Documented incident response plan with defined roles, tested annually at minimum Response plan tested quarterly via tabletop or live drill, refined from each real incident's postmortem Recover Backups exist but restoration has never been tested Documented recovery procedures, restoration tested annually Recovery time objectives defined per system criticality and verified against actual tested restoration times The assessment only has value if the scoring holds up, which is harder than it sounds when the person scoring it is also accountable for the result. Score against evidence rather than intention. "We have a policy" is evidence of intent, and it does not reach Level 3 unless the policy is followed. Ask for the artifact, the access review log, the tested restore record, the tabletop exercise notes, before accepting a self-reported level. A Level 1 or 2 in any function is a prioritization input rather than an emergency in itself. Rank functions by business impact if that function fails, rather than by how uncomfortable the low score is, and fund the highest-impact gap first rather than the easiest one to fix. A frequent gap between what a certification confirms and what an organization assumes it confirms. SOC 2 or ISO 27001 provides assurance over a defined scope and a defined audit period: that the specific controls in that scope existed and operated as described during that window. That's a narrower, bounded claim than "maturity" as this page uses the term. This ladder describes an ongoing, evolving posture across an entire function, whereas a certification is a point-in-time assurance statement about a control set the organization itself proposed for audit. That the scope covered every system that matters, that the posture is sustained after the audit period ends rather than a snapshot assembled for it, or that a novel attack pattern outside the certified controls would be caught. Treat certification as evidence for one point on the ladder; the rest of it still has to be scored. Rate each NIST CSF function 1 to 5 against the ladder above. This runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. The practical reason to run this assessment at all, beyond the framework being well known. Many regulatory frameworks, industry standards, and customer security questionnaires reference or heavily overlap with CSF 2.0's six functions, Govern especially, since regulators and procurement teams increasingly ask the governance question directly: who owns this, and how is it reported to leadership. A single NIST CSF assessment gives a reasonable starting map for gap analysis against HIPAA, PCI DSS, or a customer security questionnaire, without redoing the assessment from scratch for each one. A healthcare or payments-specific regulation has requirements that don't map cleanly onto any single CSF function, a specific breach notification timeline, a specific cardholder data handling rule. The crosswalk gets you most of the way; the remaining gap has to be checked directly against the specific regulation's text. Two maturity pages that look similar in structure but answer different questions, worth running both rather than picking one. This page scores a broad governance and lifecycle posture using a widely recognized standard, useful for board conversations, audit readiness, and mapping against specific regulatory obligations. Zero-Trust Maturity scores a specific architectural posture across six dimensions purpose-built around identity, segmentation, and blast radius, useful for engineering and security architecture decisions. The two should tell different stories about the same organization rather than duplicate the same story in different language. A team scoring well on this page's Protect function can still score poorly on zero-trust segmentation, and that gap is exactly the kind of thing worth knowing rather than averaging away.

title: Building a Security Program
description: How to stand up a security function from little or nothing, sequenced by what reduces risk first, as distinct from scoring a program that already exists.
body: Sequencing: what to build first Where security reports, and how it's funded The certification trap DevSecOps: where security enters the pipeline Building without headcount Third-party and vendor risk as part of the program The human element What the program looks like at different stages Signs the program is theater Security programs built in the wrong order spend budget on certifications before basics are solid, then fail an audit or a real incident on something the certification never checked. Stage Focus Why it sits here in the sequence Foundation MFA everywhere, least-privilege access, asset inventory, basic logging Everything else depends on this being in place rather than aspirational Visibility Centralized logging, vulnerability scanning, dependency tracking You can't manage what you can't see; this precedes any formal certification effort Process Incident response plan, vulnerability management SLA, access review cadence Turns visibility into action with defined ownership and timelines Certification SOC 2, ISO 27001, or industry-specific frameworks Documents what should already be true; pursuing it earlier produces a program built for the audit rather than for risk Organizational placement determines whether security has authority or exists to be consulted and overruled. Security leadership with a direct line to the CEO, CTO, or board, rather than buried three levels inside engineering where its priorities compete for the same budget and headcount as feature delivery and consistently lose. Funded as its own line item rather than a rounding error inside another team's budget. Security reporting to the VP of Engineering whose bonus is tied to shipping velocity, which creates a structural conflict every time a security requirement would slow a release. The person deciding the tradeoff has an incentive on only one side of it. Chasing SOC 2 or ISO 27001 before the underlying practice exists produces a certification that doesn't mean what it's supposed to mean. Treat the certification as documentation of an existing, functioning program rather than the goal itself. If the auditor's checklist is the first time a control gets implemented, it'll be the first thing that lapses once attention moves elsewhere after the audit passes. A clean SOC 2 report sitting alongside weak day-to-day practice, because the control existed for exactly the audit window and nowhere else. This is discoverable, and it's the kind of gap a technology diligence process is built to find. Security that only reviews code after it's written catches less and creates more friction than security embedded earlier. Automated scanning (SAST, dependency checking, secret detection) running in CI on every commit, with findings surfaced to the engineer who wrote the code within minutes rather than batched into a security review weeks later when context is gone and the fix costs more. A security team that reviews finished features right before release, which makes every finding an emergency, teaches engineers to see security as an obstacle rather than a partner, and pushes fixes to be rushed under deadline pressure. Early-stage companies rarely get a security team on day one. The sequencing still matters even with one part-time person or none. Start with the foundation-stage items above; they cost discipline more than headcount: enforce MFA, remove standing admin access, keep a current inventory of what systems exist and who owns them. A fractional security advisor or a well-scoped external assessment can substitute for a full-time hire through the visibility stage; process and certification need dedicated ownership once the company is large enough that a security incident would be existential. A large share of breaches now originate through a vendor rather than a direct attack on the company's own perimeter. A security program that stops at the company's own systems is scoped to the wrong boundary. Every vendor with access to production systems or sensitive data gets a security review before signing, using the same evidence-over-policy discipline covered in the certification trap above. Track which vendors hold what data, and get notification obligations for a vendor's own breach written into the contract. Security review happens for major platform vendors and gets skipped for the small SaaS tool a team signed up for with a credit card, which is exactly the kind of vendor least likely to have a mature security program and most likely to be the entry point when something goes wrong. Most incidents start with a person rather than a zero-day. Awareness training exists to address this and usually doesn't. Short, frequent, specific training tied to real incidents the company or its industry has seen, plus simulated phishing that's used to identify where more support is needed rather than to publicly shame whoever clicked. The goal is a workforce that reports a suspicious email in minutes instead of hiding a mistake. An annual training video nobody remembers a week later, run once for compliance purposes and never referenced again. It satisfies an audit requirement and does close to nothing for risk, which is the same gap the certification trap describes, applied to people instead of controls. The sequencing above holds at every size. What changes is how much of it is a dedicated person versus a shared responsibility. Stage What's realistic Under 50 engineers Foundation stage owned by engineering leadership directly, no dedicated headcount yet. A fractional advisor for anything requiring specialized judgment. 50 to 200 engineers First dedicated security hire, typically a generalist covering foundation and visibility stages. Certification work, if customer-driven, usually needs external audit support. 200 to 1,000 engineers A small team with a named leader reporting per the authority guidance above, specialization beginning (application security separate from infrastructure security). 1,000-plus engineers A full function with dedicated roles across the domains this page and Security & Compliance Maturity describe, and enough scale that the vendor risk program above needs its own owner. Patterns that show up when a security program looks complete in documentation and isn't reflected in daily operation. Policies exist and are current, but engineers can't describe what they do differently because of them A clean audit report alongside known unpatched vulnerabilities or unreviewed access grants Security reviews happen only at release time, never earlier in the development process No one can say when the last access review happened or produce evidence it occurred Security funding and headcount decisions are made by the same leader whose other priorities compete directly with security requirements Vendor security review happens for large platform contracts and gets skipped for anything signed up with a credit card

title: Understanding the System Before Changing It
description: A ten-question diagnostic for understanding a system, team, process, or technology, well enough to anticipate how it will respond before you intervene.
body: Define the system Define the boundary Identify actors Identify incentives Identify feedback loops Identify delays Identify indirect effects Identify constraints Identify measures Design the intervention, then observe the response Before you sign off on the intervention What you're changing, stated at the level where the behavior lives rather than the level where the budget line sits. Name the system being changed, and go beyond the artifact being removed or added. The artifact is the visible trigger. The system is everything whose behavior depends on it. The artifact is four reporting lines. The system being changed is every business unit president's direct influence over what used to be their own technology priorities, and the speed that came from a technology leader who sat in that president's own staff meeting every week. The artifact is an event bus. The system being changed is every point-to-point contract between the five systems, the implicit timing and ordering assumptions baked into each one, and every downstream report or reconciliation process that quietly depends on those assumptions holding. What you're excluding, and whether that exclusion makes the analysis easier or makes it wrong. Every analysis draws a boundary around what counts as "in scope." The boundary is usually drawn to make the planning tractable, which means it's drawn to exclude exactly the inconvenient parts. The boundary drawn for planning was "reporting lines and the org chart." Excluded: the commitments each business unit president already made to their own board or customers based on having direct control over technology, and the unwritten, unit-specific prioritization logic no one ever documented centrally. The boundary drawn for planning was "the integration layer." Excluded: the five system owners' own roadmaps, each of which assumed continued control over their point-to-point contracts, and the data warehouse's nightly batch jobs, which rely on a delivery order the event bus doesn't guarantee. Who behaves differently because of the intervention, beyond who signs off on it. Approval lists and stakeholder lists are not the same thing as the list of people whose day-to-day behavior changes. The second list is usually longer and less obvious. The four technology leaders now reporting to the CTO are the obvious actors. Beyond them: every business unit president who loses direct authority over what used to be their own roadmap. Every business stakeholder who now routes a request through a shared enterprise queue instead of a direct relationship with an embedded technology leader. The team building the event bus is the obvious actor. Beyond it: every system owner who now has to instrument their system to publish events instead of just responding to direct calls. Every analyst whose report assumed CRM updates arrive before billing updates, an order the bus doesn't guarantee. What behavior the current system rewards, which is usually not the same thing as what the org chart says it rewards. Every system rewards something whether anyone designed it to or not. Find the reward structure that operates in practice before assuming the intervention only changes what it was aimed at. The current system rewards each business unit's technology leader for being maximally responsive to their own president, since that's who evaluates them and controls their budget. Centralizing removes that direct incentive and replaces it with enterprise-level prioritization no single president controls, so responsiveness to any one unit necessarily drops even as total enterprise throughput rises. The current system rewards each system owner for shipping their own roadmap fast, since integrations are point-to-point and entirely theirs to manage. An event bus rewards owners for publishing stable, well-documented event contracts, a different skill than shipping features quickly. What gets amplified, what gets suppressed, once the change is live. An intervention rarely adds a new behavior in isolation. It usually strengthens one existing loop and weakens another, and the weakened loop was often doing quiet, unglamorous work. Amplified: standardization pressure, since a centralized CTO is rewarded for reducing duplicate platforms and enforcing common tooling across units. Suppressed: the fast, informal channel that let a business unit president get an urgent fix bumped to the front of the queue without a formal enterprise-wide justification. Amplified: how freely owners add new integrations, since publishing an event is cheaper than negotiating a new point-to-point contract with another team. Suppressed: the friction that used to force two teams to talk before building a new dependency between their systems. What consequences won't appear immediately, and how long the gap plausibly runs before they do. A delay is what lets a bad intervention look successful for a while. The longer the delay, the more confidently people will point to the wrong evidence when asked if it worked. For the first two quarters, the four technology leaders keep making the same calls they always did out of habit and relationship, so almost nothing visibly changes. The effect that matters, roadmap decisions increasingly reflecting enterprise tradeoffs instead of any one unit's priorities, shows up nine to twelve months later, once the centralized budget cycle runs its first full round. The event bus goes live and every system publishes correctly on day one. The cost shows up months later, when the warehouse's nightly reports start silently running on stale data during any week event delivery lags by even a few minutes, a failure mode the old synchronous calls never had. What emerges from the intervention beyond the thing it was aimed at, whether that shows up nearby, elsewhere, or later. The intended effect gets modeled because it's the point of the change. Indirect effects get missed because nobody's job was to look for them, and they don't always arrive as a single, traceable step. Sometimes it's a feedback loop producing a result much later. Sometimes it's simultaneous, showing up somewhere nobody thought to check. The goal was reducing duplicate technology spend across units. One indirect effect: business unit presidents who used to treat their technology leader as part of their own leadership team start making major business decisions with no technology input in the room, because that seat physically moved to a different reporting line and stopped showing up to their staff meeting. The goal was reducing integration maintenance burden. One indirect effect: the customer-facing app starts showing intermittent, hard-to-reproduce data inconsistencies, because two events that used to arrive in guaranteed order under a direct call now sometimes arrive out of order through the bus, a case nobody who built the original UI logic anticipated. Which constraints are binding (physics, contract, regulation) and which are organizational habits nobody has re-examined lately. Every plan runs into "we can't do that because X." Half of those X's are load-bearing. The other half are how it's always been done, restated as if it were a law of physics. Binding constraint: one business unit operates under a regulatory requirement that mandates a separately governed technology function, so that unit can't be fully centralized without a compliance problem. Habit, never questioned: the assumption that every unit needs its own full technology leadership stack rather than shared platform capability with unit-specific product ownership. Binding constraint: billing's downstream finance reporting requires transactional consistency an eventually-consistent bus can't provide without extra work. Habit, never questioned: the assumption that every integration needs to be real-time, when several of the five systems only ever needed daily reconciliation. What you're optimizing, and what behavior that specific metric will produce once people start managing to it. Whatever gets measured gets managed to, including the parts of the metric you didn't intend. State the metric, then ask what the cheapest way to hit it looks like. If the measure is "total technology headcount reduced," the cuts land hardest on whichever unit documented its context the least rather than on duplication. The metric that matters is duplicate capability eliminated without loss of unit-specific delivery speed; headcount alone measures the wrong thing. If the measure is "point-to-point integrations removed," teams migrate the easy ones first and leave the fragile, high-risk ones for later, the opposite of where the risk lives. The metric that matters is risk-weighted fragility reduced; integration count measures the wrong thing. The intervention that changes the system behavior you want with the least unnecessary disruption, rather than the largest change that feels decisive. Everything above exists to inform this design choice. A sequenced intervention that respects the loops and delays you just found usually beats a bigger one that ignores them, though a structural problem sometimes needs a structural fix rather than a smaller version of the same mistake. Either way, the intervention is never the last step. Watch what the system does in response, and update the answers above if it's not what questions 4 through 9 predicted. Instead of centralizing all four units in one reorg announcement: a phased centralization starting with the shared services duplicated identically across all four units, common infrastructure, security, while each unit keeps a dedicated technology lead in their president's staff meeting for at least two more budget cycles. Afterward, check whether presidents still report technology as represented at their leadership table, rather than assuming the org chart change was fine because nobody complained in month one. Instead of cutting all five systems over in one release: a phased migration starting with the two systems least sensitive to ordering, with the old point-to-point path kept running in parallel until event delivery is proven reliable under production load. Afterward, the warehouse's report accuracy gets checked against the old baseline rather than assumed fine because the bus is technically delivering events. Run this against any change crossing more than one team's boundary, a shared platform, or a standing risk control. You can name at least two actors, beyond the team proposing the change, who will behave differently once it ships You can name the current incentive the change removes or reverses, as well as the goal it's meant to achieve You've written down an indirect effect you expect, alongside the intended one the proposal is optimized for The success metric measures the outcome you want rather than the easiest thing to measure by the deadline You've stated which constraints are binding and which are how it's always been done, out loud, in the room

title: We're Introducing AI
description: A situational entry point for a technology leader being asked to bring AI into the enterprise: the decisions with dates, the questions that separate viable initiatives from demos, the pilot-sprawl trap, and what should exist at 30, 90, and 180 days.
body: Where to start What has to be decided, and by when Questions that separate initiatives from demos Pilot sprawl What should exist at 30, 90, and 180 days Portfolio and data first, because they decide what is feasible. Governance and architecture next, because they decide what is safe and repeatable. Cost throughout. AI Portfolio ManagementGate on feasibility and data readiness first, then classify every initiative as Scale, Incubate, Watch, or Kill. This is the page that turns a wishlist into a portfolio. Data StrategyData quality, lineage, and ownership are the prerequisite most AI programs discover after the pilot. Read this before committing to anything that depends on your own data. AI Governance MapRisk tiering, intake, human oversight, and the standards landscape: ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF, and when certification is worth it. Regulatory MapThe EU AI Act timeline after the 2026 deferral, the US state picture, and who owns each obligation. AI Architecture MapRAG, document intelligence, agent orchestration, PHI and PII protection, and observability, with provider choices at every stage. Identity & Access ArchitectureAgents act with whatever identity they are given; scope it before the first one reaches production. AI FinOps MapToken economics, reserved capacity, caching and batch discounts, and the break-even for self-hosting. Model this before the bill teaches you. AI and the Engineering Operating ModelWhat changes in how engineers work when AI tooling is in the loop, and what does not. Technology Risk AppetiteState explicitly what the organization will not accept from an AI system before someone ships it. Build vs BuyMost AI capability should be bought or composed. The page for deciding where the exceptions are. The organization is already using AI whether or not a decision has been made. These decisions replace drift with structure without slowing the work down. By when Decision Who owns it What it looks like when it goes wrong Day 7 Who owns AI in the organization: one accountable executive, a portfolio, and an intake path, so that requests have somewhere to go CEO, on the CTO's recommendation Every function starts its own initiative, nobody can say what the company is doing with AI, and the board finds out from a vendor Day 14 What is already in use, sanctioned or not, and which of it handles customer, employee, or regulated data CTO with the CISO A shadow tool with an open data-retention policy has been receiving customer records for six months Day 30 The risk tiers and the intake criteria, published, with the uses that are prohibited outright named CTO with legal and the CISO Governance arrives after the first initiative ships and is experienced as a brake rather than a lane Day 45 The first portfolio classification: which initiatives Scale, Incubate, Watch, or Kill, and what each one costs CTO with the business owners Fifteen pilots, no kills, and a budget line that nobody can trace to an outcome Day 60 The platform decision: which model providers, which hosting posture, which guardrails and observability are mandatory for anything in production CTO with the architecture function Each team picks a provider, builds its own retrieval stack, and none of it is monitorable or portable Day 90 The unit economics of the first production initiative, measured, and whether it justifies scaling CTO with the CFO The pilot's demo cost is used as the production estimate and the bill arrives at ten times the model Ask these of every proposed initiative before it gets a budget line, and again before it goes to production. For each proposed initiative, what data does it need, does it exist, who owns it, and what is its quality today Which initiatives would be valuable if they worked, and which are being proposed because they are visible What is the organization's tolerance for a wrong answer in this use case, and who has said so Which of the current AI tools in use retain or train on the data sent to them, and what has been sent Where does a human review the output, and is that review substantive or a checkbox What does the first initiative cost per transaction at production volume rather than demo volume Which regulations already apply to the decisions the AI will influence, regardless of the fact that it is AI If the model provider changed pricing, terms, or availability tomorrow, what would break and how fast could it be swapped What would the organization stop doing if this initiative succeeded, and does anyone want to stop doing it The most common state of an enterprise AI program at month nine is a dozen pilots, each with a champion, none with a kill criterion, and no way to say which of them the company is betting on. Every function got a pilot approved because saying no felt like being against AI. Each one used a different provider, built its own prompt library, and stored its own copy of the data. Six are technically working, none are in production, the cost is now visible on the cloud bill, and the board asks what the company got for it. The answer is a set of demos. Run it as a portfolio from day one, with the gating in AI Portfolio Management: feasibility and data readiness before anything else, an explicit Kill classification that is used, and a cap on concurrent incubations. Pay for the platform layer once, centrally: guardrails, observability, retrieval, and cost attribution. Measure unit economics on the first production initiative before scaling anything, and report the portfolio to the board as a portfolio, including the kills. A program that can show these artifacts is a program the board can fund with confidence. One that cannot is a set of pilots. Checkpoint What exists Day 30 One accountable owner and a published intake path. An inventory of AI tools already in use, with data exposure classified. Risk tiers and prohibited uses published. The first version of the risk appetite statement covering AI systems. Day 90 A classified portfolio with costs, owners, and kill criteria. A platform decision recorded as an ADR: providers, hosting posture, mandatory guardrails and observability. The data readiness gaps for the Scale and Incubate initiatives named with owners. At least one initiative killed, publicly, so the organization learns the classification has teeth. Day 180 The first production initiative live, with measured unit economics and a monitored error rate, reported to the board. Cost attribution by initiative on the bill. A governance process that has processed real intake and can show its decisions. A one-page AI narrative for the board that describes a portfolio rather than a pile of pilots.

title: We're Cutting Costs
description: A situational entry point for a technology cost reduction mandate: the decisions with dates, the questions that separate real savings from deferred cost, the across-the-board trap, and what should exist at 30, 60, and 90 days.
body: Where to start What has to be decided, and by when Questions that separate savings from deferred cost The across-the-board percentage What should exist at 30, 60, and 90 days Framing first, then the ranked list, then the CFO. The mechanics of cloud and vendor savings come after the decisions about what is protected. Technology Strategy During a DownturnThe framing for the whole exercise: what to protect, what to pause, and what to kill, decided before the spreadsheet opens. Technology Capital AllocationThe pre-ranked cut list this moment demands. If it does not exist yet, this page is how to build it in a week. Working with the CFONumbers with visible derivation, and the conversation that has to happen before the budget meeting rather than in it. Running the Technology BudgetWhere the money goes today, at a level of detail the CFO will trust. Cloud FinOpsUsually the fastest savings that stick: rightsizing, commitment coverage, waste elimination, and showback so it does not creep back. Application Portfolio ManagementThe TIME map turns a vague desire to retire things into a named list with owners and dates. Technical Debt EconomicsWhich debt to keep carrying and which to fund, as numbers, so the cut does not land on the item with the highest carry cost. Vendor EvaluationExit cost and renewal leverage for the contracts that make up most of the non-people spend. SaaS Contract & Renewal NegotiationThe renewal calendar and the clauses to fix; usually the largest non-recurring saving available. Innovation Portfolio ManagementWhich bets survive and which get paused explicitly rather than starved quietly. Platform EngineeringWhere consolidation reduces both cost and cognitive load, and where it only moves the cost somewhere less visible. A cost mandate has a clock on it from the day it lands. These are the decisions that determine whether the cut is a plan or a scramble. By when Decision Who owns it What it looks like when it goes wrong Day 3 Which categories are protected outright, before any line-item review begins: security baseline, regulatory obligations, the systems that make revenue CTO, agreed with the CEO Everything is negotiable, so the loudest advocates protect their budgets and the quiet ones absorb the cut Day 7 Whether the target is achievable without headcount, and if not, what the headcount number is and where it lands CTO with the CFO and CHRO A tooling-only plan is presented, misses by half, and a headcount cut arrives late and unplanned Day 14 The ranked cut list, with the consequence of each item stated plainly, delivered to the CFO one-on-one CTO The list is revealed for the first time in the budget meeting and every line becomes a fight Day 21 Which vendor renewals in the next twelve months get renegotiated, consolidated, or exited, and who runs each negotiation CTO with procurement Contracts auto-renew at list price during the exact quarter the company is cutting Day 30 Which in-flight initiatives stop, pause with a restart condition, or continue at reduced scope CTO with the CEO Nothing is stopped, everything is slowed, and every initiative misses Day 45 How savings are tracked and reported, and who signs off that a saving is a reduction rather than a deferral CTO with finance Savings are declared at the announcement and never reconciled, and the cost comes back within a year Most cost plans fail because nobody asked whether the saving is a reduction, a deferral, or a transfer. Ask these before any number goes to the CFO. What is the run cost of the estate, by system, and how much of it is licensing that scales with headcount you are about to reduce Which applications on the TIME map are already marked tolerate or eliminate, and what has stopped them being retired so far How much of cloud spend is uncommitted on-demand, and how much of the committed spend is under-utilized Which contracts renew in the next twelve months, at what value, and with what notice period For every proposed saving, is it a reduction in run cost, a deferral of spend that returns later, or a transfer of cost to another team or the business What is the cost of the next major incident, and does the proposed cut increase its probability Which roles, if cut, remove the only person who understands a system that still makes money What does the security program lose, specifically, and does that change the stated risk appetite What would the team stop doing if headcount were reduced, and has anyone written that list down The most common way to cut technology cost is to apply the same percentage to every team and category. It protects nothing that matters and reflects no prioritization; it avoids the discomfort of choosing. Every team loses fifteen percent. Security loses its pen test budget, the platform team loses the engineer who was automating the thing that costs the most, and the revenue-critical system's on-call rota drops to two people. Nine months later the run cost is back where it was, the deferred work is more expensive, and the best people have left because they could see nothing was being decided. Decide the protected categories first, then cut deeper in fewer places. Retire whole systems rather than trimming every system. Take the vendor renewals seriously; they are usually the largest non-recurring saving available. Report savings only when they show up in the ledger, and keep the ranked list alive after the cut so the next round, if it comes, is already answered. The announcement is the easy part. These are the artifacts that make the saving stick and hold up to scrutiny. Checkpoint What exists Day 30 A protected-category list agreed with the CEO. A ranked cut list with consequences stated, already reviewed by the CFO privately. A vendor renewal calendar for the next twelve months with a strategy per contract. An explicit stop, pause, and continue decision for every in-flight initiative. Day 60 Cloud commitment coverage and rightsizing actions executed, with the saving visible in the bill rather than in a forecast. The first vendor renegotiations closed. Headcount decisions, if any, made and communicated once rather than in waves. A written record of what the organization has stopped doing. Day 90 A savings tracker reconciled against actual spend, signed by finance. A restart condition recorded for every paused initiative. The security and reliability posture re-stated against the new spend level so nobody is surprised later. The next round of cuts, if asked for, answered from the same list rather than from scratch.

title: The Company Is Growing Rapidly
description: A situational entry point for the technology leader of a company that is scaling fast: the decisions that have to be made before the org doubles, the questions that reveal what will break next, the hiring-as-a-fix trap, and what should exist at 30, 90, and 180 days.
body: Where to start What has to be decided, and by when Questions that reveal what breaks next Hiring as the fix for every constraint What should exist at 30, 90, and 180 days The systems lens first, because growth problems are constraint problems. Then structure and people, then the platform and architecture decisions that stop ten teams from becoming ten companies. Systems Thinking for CTOsGrowth is a systems problem. Which constraint binds next is the question, and this is the lens for finding it. Org DesignTeam topology, span of control, and the point at which the structure that got you here starts costing you. Technical Hiring & LevelingA leveling framework before the headcount doubles, or every new hire is negotiated from scratch and the existing team notices. Engineering CultureWhat gets rewarded changes as the company grows, usually without anyone deciding it should. Platform EngineeringThe moment team count outgrows the ability of every team to run its own infrastructure, and what to build instead. Observability & SRE Operating ModelDecide who is on call and what the reliability function owns before the team count doubles. Integration & API PatternsThe small set of integration rules that stop ten teams from becoming ten incompatible systems. Architecture Review BoardLightweight, evidence-based review before ten teams make ten incompatible decisions about the same thing. Engineering MetricsThe handful of numbers that tell you delivery is degrading before the customers do. Enterprise ArchitectureWhen to stand up an EA function, at what size, and the ways it fails if stood up too early or too heavily. Agile and SAFeWhether scaled frameworks help, and the point at which adopting one is a substitute for making decisions. Building a Security ProgramCustomers, auditors, and regulators arrive with growth. The security program has to be ahead of them. Identity & Access ArchitectureJoiner, mover, leaver automated from the HR source before the hiring wave, or offboarding fails silently at scale. Reliability as an Economic DecisionThe reliability the business needs at ten times the volume is a different number, and it has a price. Growth makes every deferred structural decision more expensive. These are sequenced by when they start to cost you if left unmade. By when Decision Who owns it What it looks like when it goes wrong Day 14 The leveling framework and compensation bands, agreed with the CEO and CHRO, before the next hiring wave CTO Every hire negotiates a title and salary independently, the existing team finds out, and the best of them leave Day 30 The team structure for the next doubling rather than the current size: what splits, what stays, who leads the new teams CTO Teams grow to fifteen people, a manager has twelve reports, and delivery slows while everyone is technically busy Day 45 The engineering metrics the leadership team will watch, and the thresholds that trigger action CTO with engineering managers Delivery degrades for two quarters and the first signal is a customer escalation Day 60 Whether to fund a platform team now, and what it owns versus what stays with product teams CTO with the CFO Every team runs its own CI, infra, and on-call, and the third outage of the quarter is caused by drift between them Day 90 The architecture decisions that must be made once, centrally: identity, data model boundaries, service standards, and the review path for exceptions CTO with the architecture function Ten teams, four languages, three message buses, and an integration problem that costs a year to unwind Day 120 The security and compliance posture the next tier of customers will require, and the timeline to get there CTO with the CISO and sales leadership A seven-figure deal stalls on a security questionnaire the company cannot answer well Growth failures are predictable if someone is looking. These are what to look at. Which single system, team, or person is the constraint on delivery today, and what is the next one after it How many people report to each engineering manager, and how many managers have never managed before What is the ratio of new hires to people who have been here more than a year, per team Which of the current processes exist because someone decided, and which exist because nobody did How long does it take a new engineer to ship to production, and what is that number's trend What is the change failure rate and recovery time, and is anyone looking at them weekly Which architectural decisions have already been made three different ways by three different teams What breaks first at ten times the current volume, and has anyone tested it What does the next tier of customers or the next market require in security, compliance, or residency that the company does not have today Which of the founders' informal roles need to become someone's job When the company is growing, the default response to any delivery problem is headcount. It is the fix that requires no structural decision, and it makes most structural problems worse. Delivery slows. Twenty engineers are hired. Onboarding consumes the senior engineers, span of control passes ten, the architecture drifts because nobody has time to review anything, and delivery per engineer halves. The headcount doubled and the output did not move. The board sees a cost line that grew faster than revenue. Find the binding constraint before hiring into it, using the approach in Systems Thinking for CTOs and Understanding the System Before Changing It. Fix structure first: leveling, team boundaries, a platform layer, a review path. Then hire into a shape that can absorb people. Watch delivery per engineer as a leading indicator, and be willing to slow hiring when it falls. Structure that is ready before the people arrive, and numbers that show whether it is working. Checkpoint What exists Day 30 A leveling framework and bands published internally. A team structure for the next doubling, with named leads and a hiring plan against it. A one-page list of the current binding constraints, ranked. The four or five engineering metrics that will be reviewed weekly, with a baseline. Day 90 A platform team funded or a recorded decision not to, with the trigger that would change it. The Architecture Review Board running, lightly. The architecture decisions that must be made once recorded as ADRs. A first-line manager development path, because most of the new managers have never done it. Day 180 Delivery per engineer stable or improving through the hiring wave. The security and compliance roadmap the next customer tier requires, funded and underway. Onboarding time to first production change measured and falling. A candid culture read, because what the company rewards has changed and someone should have decided how.

title: We Just Had a Major Incident
description: A situational entry point for the days after a major incident: what to decide in the first 72 hours, the questions to ask before the postmortem, the trap that turns a recoverable incident into a credibility problem, and what should exist at 7, 30, and 90 days.
body: Where to start What has to be decided, and by when Questions to ask before the postmortem Fixing the incident instead of the class of incident What should exist at 7, 30, and 90 days Run the response first. The reflection and communication work matters just as much once the fire is out, and it is where most of the lasting damage is done or avoided. Incident ResponseDetection through postmortem follow-through, with the failure modes that turn a manageable incident chaotic. Regulatory MapWhich reporting clocks started when you became aware, and who owns each one. Data Governance & PrivacyIf any personal or regulated data was involved, which notification regimes apply and which clocks started the moment you became aware. Board ReportingCommunicating what happened upward without making it worse, and the out-of-cycle escalation path that should already exist. Epistemology & Research MethodsRoot cause versus triggering event, and the correlation-versus-causation trap that produces confident, wrong postmortems. Technology Risk AppetiteWas this a risk the organization meant to accept, or a gap in the stated appetite itself. Observability & SRE Operating ModelIf detection was slow or the same few people carried the response, the operating model is the finding. Reliability as an Economic DecisionTurn the incident's cost into the number that decides the next reliability investment. Disaster Recovery & Business ContinuityIf this was bigger than a single incident: recovery testing, RTO/RPO, and what the board will ask next. These decisions do not wait for the postmortem. Deferring them is itself a decision, usually the wrong one. By when Decision Who owns it What it looks like when it goes wrong Hour 4 Is this potentially material, reportable, or customer-notifiable, and which clocks have started CTO with counsel and the CISO The 72-hour breach notification window and the materiality assessment are discovered on day three Hour 24 What customers, the board, and the company are told, in what words, by whom CEO, with the CTO supplying the facts and the timeline Three different stories reach three audiences and the least accurate one reaches the press Day 3 Whether the immediate fix is stable enough to stand down the war room and return to normal operations Incident commander, ratified by the CTO The war room runs for two weeks because nobody is willing to say the residual risk is acceptable Day 7 Who runs the postmortem, who attends, and whether it is blameless in practice rather than in name CTO The postmortem is run by the team that owns the failed system and produces action items only for that team Day 14 Which postmortem actions get funded now, from what, and which are consciously deferred with a date CTO with the CFO Forty actions, none funded, all still open at the next incident Day 30 Whether the incident changes the stated risk appetite, the DR posture, or the operating model CTO with the CEO and board The organization spends on the specific failure and leaves the class of failure untouched Answers the CTO should have before sitting in the room. The postmortem is for the team to learn; these are for the CTO to understand what kind of organization had this incident. How long between the failure beginning and someone knowing, and was that someone a customer How many people could have run this response, and how many did Was any part of the recovery dependent on a single person's knowledge, credentials, or access Did the runbook exist, was it current, and was it used Did any monitoring fire before the impact, and if so, why was it not acted on Which contributing conditions were known and previously deprioritized, and where is that decision recorded What did the response cost in engineering time, cloud spend, credits, and customer concessions, in dollars Which customer contracts carry notification, service credit, or termination clauses that this incident triggered Was the last restore or failover test for this class of system run in the past twelve months, and did it pass The most common outcome of a major incident is a well-executed fix for the specific failure, with the conditions that produced it left in place. The database failover that did not work gets tested and fixed. The fact that no failover in the estate has been tested in two years is not raised, because the postmortem's scope was the incident. Six months later a different failover fails, and this time the board asks why the first one did not prompt the question. One question in every postmortem, asked by the CTO personally: where else in the estate does this same condition exist. The answer becomes a separate item with its own owner, funded from the reserve in Capital Allocation, and reported to the board as the remediation that matters. The specific fix is table stakes; the class-level answer is the leadership output. The postmortem document is the least of it. Checkpoint What exists Day 7 A written timeline with detection, escalation, and recovery times stated in minutes rather than adjectives. A completed regulatory and contractual notification log. A one-page summary for the board in the form the Board Reporting page describes. The postmortem scheduled with the right attendees, including someone from outside the owning team. Day 30 The postmortem published internally, with actions that have owners, dates, and funding decisions. The class-of-incident question answered with a list. A recorded decision on whether the risk appetite or DR posture changes. If detection or response depended on too few people, an operating model change proposed with a cost attached. Day 90 The funded actions closed or visibly progressing against their dates. A restore or failover test run on the class of system that failed. The incident's cost stated in dollars and used in the next reliability investment conversation. The board updated once more, unprompted, which is what turns a bad quarter into evidence of control.

title: We're Going Through M&A
description: A situational entry point for technology leaders on either side of a transaction: what to decide before and after close, the questions that reprice or stop a deal, the integration trap most frameworks skip, and what should exist at Day 0, 30, and 100.
body: Where to start What has to be decided, and by when Questions that reprice or stop a deal Diligence that stops at the slides What should exist at diligence close, Day 30, and Day 100 Diligence pages first, then integration, then the people and decision-rights pages that determine whether the combined organization can function. Technology DiligenceTechnical debt signals, key-person risk, security posture, and the red flags that should stop or reprice a deal. M&A Diligence KitThe question bank, the data room structure, and the sell-side preparation sequence. Application Portfolio ManagementScore the target's estate on the same TIME map as your own so the integration decisions are made on one view instead of two. Technology M&A IntegrationDay 0 continuity, the converge, coexist, or replace decision, and the execution phase that determines whether synergies materialize. CTO Leadership & SuccessionKey-person retention on both sides; the people who matter most are the ones who can leave fastest. Technology Decision RightsTwo organizations means two sets of decision owners. Make the combined ones explicit before the first conflict. Role Boundaries: CTO, CIO, CISO, CPOWhich executive owns what in the combined organization, decided before day one rather than discovered in month three. Data Governance & PrivacyCustomer data crossing entity and jurisdiction boundaries has legal consequences that integration plans routinely ignore. Security & Compliance MaturityThe target's certifications tell you what was audited, which is a narrower claim than what is true. Score on evidence before you inherit the gap. Identity & Access ArchitectureThe privileged account export is the one artifact that tells you how the target ran security; pull it in diligence and again on Day 0. Regulatory MapWhich regimes follow the data and the entities across the transaction, and which notifications the deal itself triggers. The clock runs from before the letter of intent through Day 100. Most of the value is decided before close and most of the damage happens in the first thirty days after it. By when Decision Who owns it What it looks like when it goes wrong Before LOI Which technology findings would stop the deal, which would reprice it, and which are integration cost to be modeled CTO with the deal team Every finding is treated as an integration detail and the price never moves Diligence week 1 Who from technology is on the diligence team, and whether they have access to the code, the cloud bill, and the people rather than a data room of slides CTO Diligence is done from an architecture deck and a SOC 2 letter, and the estate as it stands is discovered post-close Diligence close The integration approach per major system: converge, coexist, or replace, with a cost and a date for each CTO with the integration lead The approach is left for the 100-day plan and the 100-day plan is spent arguing about it Signing Which named people must be retained, with what terms, and who has the conversation with them before the announcement CTO with the CEO and CHRO The two engineers who understand the billing system hear about the deal from the press and resign in week two Day 0 What must not break on day one: identity, payroll, customer-facing systems, security monitoring across both estates CTO, run as an incident-style operation A domain trust or SSO change on day one locks out half the acquired company Day 30 The combined decision-rights and executive role map, published CTO with the CEO Two CISOs, two platform teams, and two roadmaps, each assuming the other will yield Day 100 Which synergy commitments are on track, which are not, and what the board is told about the difference CTO with the CFO The synergy number from the deal model is reported as if it were a plan rather than an assumption Ask these in diligence, of the target's engineers and their cloud bill rather than their slides. What percentage of the target's revenue depends on systems that fewer than three people understand What does the target's cloud bill look like by service and by month, and how does it compare to what was presented How many production incidents in the last year, how were they detected, and how long did recovery take Which of the target's certifications are in scope for the systems that matter to the deal thesis Where does customer and employee data physically live, under which entity, and which regulations follow it across the transaction Which contracts have change-of-control clauses, and which vendors gain pricing leverage the day the deal closes What is the target's technical debt, as a scored backlog rather than a paragraph of reassurance Who on the target's side has been told the truth about their role post-close, and who has not If the acquired product is to be replaced, what is the realistic migration cost and timeline, and who has done one of these before The most expensive M&A technology failure is a diligence exercise that reads the target's own description of itself and moves on, because the deal team is under time pressure and the technology findings are not seen as price-moving. The target presents a clean architecture diagram, a SOC 2 Type II, and a roadmap. Post-close, the platform turns out to depend on a single contractor, the SOC 2 scope excluded the product that drove the valuation, and the integration cost is three times the model. None of this was hidden. Nobody asked for the artifact. Treat diligence as an evidence exercise using the same discipline as Epistemology & Research Methods: for every claim, ask for the artifact, and treat the absence of one as the finding. Insist that specific technology findings appear in the price and the terms as well as the integration plan. Then run Day 0 like an incident and the first 100 days like a program with a tracker rather than a set of good intentions. The deal model is a set of assumptions. These are the artifacts that turn it into a plan and then into a result. Checkpoint What exists Diligence close A scored technology diligence report with red flags classified as stop, reprice, or integration cost. A TIME map of the target's estate. A named key-person list with retention actions. A per-system converge, coexist, or replace decision with cost and date. Specific technology findings reflected in the price, the reps and warranties, or the escrow. Day 30 Day 0 completed without a customer-facing or identity outage. The combined executive role and decision-rights map published. Retention conversations held with every named individual. Change-of-control vendor contracts triaged. A single security monitoring view across both estates, even if crude. Day 100 An integration tracker reporting synergy realization against the deal model, with variance explained. The first replace or converge migration either underway with a plan or explicitly re-scoped. The board told which synergy assumptions were wrong and what replaces them. Nobody critical lost by surprise.

title: I'm Starting as CTO
description: A curated reading order for the first 90 days rather than a comprehensive list. Every link below points to a full page elsewhere on this site.
body: Where to start The reading list is sequenced. The role runs in parallel. Reading what you're told as well as what you're shown What good looks like at 30, 60, and 90 days The Wharton CTO Program Roughly sequenced: assessment first, then the relationships and structure that determine whether anything you decide sticks. Technology DiligenceEven without an acquisition, this is the lens for assessing what you've inherited. Application Portfolio ManagementBuild the TIME map of what's running before you propose changing any of it. Technology Decision RightsGet decision ownership explicit before ambiguity costs you in your first quarter. Identity & Access ArchitecturePull the privileged role export in week one; it is the fastest reliable read of the security posture you inherited. Technical Debt EconomicsTurn the debt complaints you will hear into three numbers per item before anyone asks you to fund them. Architecture Review BoardStand up evidence-based review early, before the first big cross-team decision gets made informally by default. Working with the CEOThe relationship that determines whether anything else on this list works. Working with the CFOWhere the budget conversation gets litigated; build this relationship before you need it defended. Engineering CultureAssess what's rewarded rather than what the values deck says, before you inherit a culture problem silently. CTO Leadership & SuccessionFind out on day one who runs things if you're out, before you need the answer. The CTO Operating SystemSet your own cadence before you're consumed entirely by everyone else's. Technology Risk AppetiteState what you won't accept before you inherit someone else's silent tolerance for it. Regulatory MapKnow which reporting clocks the company is on before the first incident teaches you. Board ReportingYour first board meeting will arrive faster than the 90-day mark suggests. Working the list above gets you moving. The full shape of what you're now responsible for is wider. The CTO Operating System maps the complete set of responsibility areas, technology strategy, architecture, team and organization, capital allocation, risk and security, executive relationships, delivery oversight, hands-on technical work, plus how the balance of time across them shifts as the organization scales. Read the list above to get moving this week. Read that page once, early, to see the whole board you're now playing on, so nothing on it comes as a surprise in month four. Every new CTO inherits a set of claims, stated with total confidence by people who may or may not have checked. See Epistemology & Research Methods for the full framework; this is what it looks like applied to your first thirty days. What you'll hear What to check What silence tells you "We don't have a technical debt problem" Ask for the artifact: an APM score, a tracked debt backlog No artifact means nobody's measured it, which is itself the finding "Our deployments are reliable" Ask for the measured change failure rate and MTTR trend A confident claim with no number behind it is an opinion wearing a fact's clothing "The team's in good shape" Check attrition, specifically regretted attrition, and referral rate Revealed preference beats a manager's felt sense every time "This vendor's solid, never an issue" Ask when it was last tested: an outage, a security review Untested reliability is luck that hasn't run out yet "Security posture is strong" Ask for the artifact: last pen test, the access review log A policy document is evidence of intent; practice needs its own evidence None of this is about assuming bad faith. Most people repeating these claims believe them, and often inherited the belief from someone else who never checked either. The habit worth building in the first month is asking for the artifact before accepting the sentence. Suspicion is a different thing and not required. The reading list above tells you what to study. This is what should exist by each checkpoint, beyond what you should have read about. Day 30 A technology and application inventory built from the systems rather than from the org chart's idea of them. A first-pass decision-rights map, even in draft. Key-person and succession risk named specifically rather than assumed to be fine. A standing weekly cadence already running with both the CEO and the CFO. Day 60 The application portfolio scored as well as inventoried. The Architecture Review Board holding its first review. A candid read on what the culture rewards, distinct from what the values deck says. A first draft of where the organization's risk appetite sits, even where it's never been stated out loud. Day 90 A stated technology strategy, written down rather than held as quiet intentions in your own head. A first board narrative delivered well rather than merely survived. A first pass at capital allocation priorities, ranked rather than only discussed. Some of the first year is solvable by reading. The rest is solved by having peers going through the same thing at the same time. Most of what's hard about the first year in this role is the judgment calls nobody else in the building has faced before, and very little of it is technical. A structured peer cohort helps precisely because everyone in it is working through the same category of problem in parallel, at a different company, which makes their notes worth comparing against your own. Wharton's Chief Technology Officer Program is a substantive program if you can make the time for it: cohort-based, built around applying the material to your own organization rather than abstract case studies, and the peer network it builds tends to outlast the program itself. Worth a look: Wharton Executive Education, Chief Technology Officer Program.

title: Stakeholder Engagement
body: Influence-interest mapping Plot your own stakeholders The placement mistake that breaks the plan Building the engagement plan itself Handling the high-influence, low-interest stakeholder The engagement plan, one row per stakeholder A platform migration with six stakeholders When the map changes The map built once, by one person, in private The foundation the engagement plan gets built on. Placing a stakeholder wrong on this grid is the most common reason an engagement plan fails before it starts. Quadrant Definition Engagement approach High influence, high interest Can materially help or block the initiative and is already paying attention to it Manage closely; regular direct engagement, involve in key decisions before they're finalized High influence, low interest Can materially affect the outcome but isn't currently engaged with the details Keep satisfied; concise, infrequent updates focused on what matters to them specifically rather than a full status report Low influence, high interest Cares a great deal but has limited power to change the outcome Keep informed; regular updates, a working channel for input, without over-indexing decisions on their preferences Low influence, low interest Neither able nor inclined to affect the outcome Monitor; minimal effort, don't manufacture engagement they haven't asked for Add a name and score influence and interest 1 to 5 each. The quadrant and strategy are computed automatically, same thresholds as above: 1 to 2 is low, 3 to 5 is high on both axes. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. Where influence-interest mapping most often goes wrong, before the engagement plan itself is even built. Placing someone by their org chart position instead of their influence over this specific initiative. A senior title doesn't guarantee influence over a given decision, and a mid-level person who controls a critical dependency can have more practical influence than their title suggests. Score influence against the specific decision at hand rather than general organizational seniority: who can delay, block, or accelerate this particular initiative, and who has the budget, headcount, or technical dependency that makes them load-bearing here. The map tells you where someone sits. The plan is what you do about it, and this is where most stakeholder work stops short. Named owner per stakeholder (not "the team"), defined cadence matched to their quadrant, the specific message or ask for each touchpoint, and a trigger for when their quadrant placement should be re-evaluated, since influence and interest both shift as an initiative progresses. Re-evaluating placement over time. A stakeholder who started low-interest often becomes high-interest once the initiative starts visibly affecting their team, and a plan built once at kickoff and never revisited misses that shift until it becomes a problem. The quadrant most engagement plans get wrong in practice, since the instinct is to either over-engage or ignore them entirely. Sending this stakeholder the same detailed weekly update everyone else gets. They tune out, and then when a decision needs their sign-off, they have no context and the ask lands as a surprise, which damages trust right at the moment you need it most. A short, infrequent update translated into what matters to them specifically, budget impact for a finance stakeholder, risk exposure for legal, timeline impact for a dependent team, in place of a general status report. When you do need something from them, it lands as a continuation of an existing thread rather than a cold ask. The grid is the diagnosis. This is the treatment, and the columns are the ones that get left blank when a plan is built to satisfy a template rather than to run an initiative. Column What goes in it What a weak entry looks like Stakeholder and role in this initiative The person, and specifically what they control here: budget, a dependency, a sign-off, a team whose work changes Their job title Quadrant and why The placement and the one sentence that justifies it against this decision The placement alone What they care about Their measure of success and their fear, in their words if you have heard them What you assume they care about What you need from them The specific decision, resource, or absence of objection, with a date Support Owner One named person on your side who holds the relationship The team, or the PMO Cadence and channel How often, in what form, one-on-one or in a forum Weekly status email Next touchpoint and message The next specific conversation and the point it needs to land TBD Re-evaluation trigger The event that would move them on the grid: a reorg, a budget cycle, the initiative touching their team None The mapping exercise that finds the stakeholder the org chart missed. A migration of the core customer platform to a new cloud environment. The initial map, drawn by the program manager from the org chart, placed the CFO and the COO as high influence, high interest; two VPs as high influence, low interest; the head of customer support as low influence, high interest; and the compliance manager as low influence, low interest. The plan was built around the two executives. Six weeks in, the migration stalled: the compliance manager had not approved the data residency change and would not be rushed, and the head of support had quietly briefed the COO that the cutover window would hit peak call volume. Scored against the decision rather than the org chart, the compliance manager is high influence (a hard dependency with a veto) and needed managing closely from week one. The head of support is high influence through the COO, and needed a direct channel rather than updates. One of the two VPs turned out to have no stake in the outcome at all and was moved to monitor. The corrected plan added two named relationships and removed one. The migration cut over eight weeks late, which is what mis-placement of two people cost, and the engagement plan was re-scored at every phase gate after that. Influence and interest move. The plan has to say when to look again, because nobody re-scores a stakeholder map on instinct. A phase gate: at each one, re-score every stakeholder against the next phase's decisions rather than the last one's A reorganization, a new executive, or a change in who owns a dependency The initiative starts visibly affecting a team that was previously low interest; they will move to high interest and usually to high influence through whoever they report to A budget cycle: finance stakeholders move quadrant when the initiative's cost appears on a review A public setback: an incident or a missed milestone raises the interest of everyone who was keeping a distance A quiet stakeholder goes silent for two consecutive touchpoints; silence from a high-influence stakeholder is a signal rather than a convenience A stakeholder map is a set of judgments about people. Built alone, it reflects one person's view of the organization; kept private, it never gets corrected. The program manager draws the grid at kickoff, files it in the project folder, and runs the plan from memory. Nobody with a different view of the organization ever sees it. The placements are wrong in the ways one person's placements are always wrong, and the errors surface as surprises rather than as corrections. Build the map in a room with three people who see the organization from different angles: the sponsor, the delivery lead, and someone from the function most affected. Disagreement about a placement is the useful output; it means someone knows something the others do not. Keep the plan visible to the core team, re-score at every gate, and treat it as a living record of what you know about who can move this initiative. The Technology Decision Rights map is the natural cross-check: anyone with an A or an R on the relevant decisions belongs on the grid.

title: Systems Thinking for CTOs
description: Interconnectedness, emergence, nonlinearity, feedback loops, delays, boundaries, and leverage points, applied to the six stages of Decision Architecture.
body: The vocabulary Interconnectedness and emergence Analysis, synthesis, and purpose Where the behavior comes from Causality loops back on itself Nonlinearity: why small causes don't stay small Local optimization vs. system optimization Delays and second-order effects Where to intervene: leverage points What this changes at each stage of Decision Architecture Signs you're treating a system as an isolated component Five structural terms, used consistently through the rest of this page and in Seeing the System Before Changing It. Term What it is Where it shows up Stock A quantity sitting somewhere at a point in time Backlog size, technical debt, headcount, cash runway, open incidents Flow The rate something moves into or out of a stock Deploy frequency, hiring rate, ticket close rate, burn rate Feedback loop A stock's own level changing the flows into or out of it Rising technical debt slows delivery, which raises pressure to cut corners, which raises technical debt further Delay The gap between a flow changing and the stock visibly responding A hiring freeze today doesn't register as reduced capacity for months Boundary What's included in the analysis, and what's assumed to hold constant Scoping a migration as "infrastructure cost" leaves the compliance exposure it also creates outside the analysis Two properties of any system that don't show up when you look at one part of it in isolation. Every stock and flow in a technology organization feeds or drains others across whatever boundary a team or org chart draws. A dependency on an architecture diagram is a channel this travels through, well beyond a documentation artifact. A change to authentication latency doesn't stay inside the identity team's service; it slows every login-gated feature across the product, and shows up as a conversion drop on a dashboard the identity team never looks at. Some properties belong to the system as a whole and don't exist at the level of any single component: reliability, delivery speed, and security posture belong to no single team; they're produced by how every team's work interacts. A postmortem that traces an outage to "the database team's mistake" is looking at one component. The outage was produced by how the database, the retry logic three services away, and a five-minute alerting delay interacted together. None of the three was broken on its own. Two different ways to understand a system, and why the second one finds things the first one can't. Breaks a system into its parts to understand how each one works. Useful, and the default: to understand why a service is slow, open the service and trace the request path. Analysis explains the mechanism inside the boundary. Understands a system by its role in the larger system that contains it rather than by taking it apart. A platform team is understood by what the product organization needs from it that no other team provides, and cataloging its services tells you little about that. Synthesis explains why the boundary was drawn where it was. Two ways to trace the same incident back to a cause, and why they land on different fixes. Treats the thing in front of you (a service, a team, a budget line) as the unit of analysis. Optimize the component, ship the fix, move on. This is the default mode most engineering organizations run in, because it matches how work gets assigned and measured. Treats the component as one node in a structure of stocks, flows, and delays connecting it to everything around it. The question becomes what changed, and for whom, rather than whether this one number improved. A caching layer that cuts latency for one service can push load onto a shared database three other teams depend on. The component fix worked. The system got worse. A cause rarely produces one effect and stops. It loops back through reinforcing and balancing structures, and the next two cards cover what that loop does to timing and scale. Amplify a direction already in motion. A team ships fast, gets praised, ships faster, cuts more corners to keep the pace, ships faster still. Nothing in the loop signals a problem until the corners cut become an incident. Pull a system back toward a target, and the target is often implicit rather than stated. An SRE team paged constantly starts declining marginal features regardless of what the roadmap says, because the loop pulling toward fewer pages is stronger than the one pulling toward shipping the roadmap. A system's response to a change is often out of proportion to the size of the change, in both directions. A growing stock, queue depth, technical debt, on-call fatigue, can grow for months with no visible symptom at all, because the system still has enough slack to absorb it. The growth looks free. It is using up a buffer nobody's watching. A service handles rising request volume with flat latency for months, because the queue drains fully between traffic peaks. The same linear month-over-month growth crosses the point where the queue stops draining between peaks, and latency goes from flat to climbing within a single week. The growth rate never changed. The system's response to it did. The tension that shows up in nearly every cross-team resourcing fight, usually without anyone naming it that way. Local optimization looks like System optimization looks like Each team hits its own velocity and cost targets The end-to-end delivery pipeline gets faster, even if one team's metrics look worse A platform team ships features for its biggest internal customer first A platform team ships the golden path that reduces total organizational toil Security reviews every change with equal rigor Security calibrates rigor to blast radius, so low-risk changes move fast and high-risk ones get close scrutiny Cost is optimized service by service Cost is optimized against the business outcome the services jointly produce The consequence that doesn't show up until long after the decision that caused it, by which point the connection is no longer obvious to anyone in the room. Technical debt taken on during a growth push doesn't slow anything down immediately; that's the point of taking it on. The cost shows up eighteen months later as declining delivery velocity that gets diagnosed as a hiring problem or a process problem, because the original decision is long forgotten and the delay severed the visible link between cause and effect. A company consolidates from four cloud accounts to one to simplify billing and governance. Immediate effect: cleaner cost reporting, faster procurement. Second-order effect, visible eight months later: every team now shares the same service quotas and blast radius, so an incident in one product line throttles API limits for every other product line sharing the account. The consolidation was correct. Nobody mapped the coupling it created before shipping it. The same amount of effort produces wildly different results depending on which piece of the structure it's aimed at. Ranked from weakest to strongest.
