The 180-day mark matters because it is roughly when a credible alternative can still be evaluated. Once the vendor knows you cannot switch before the renewal date, the negotiation is about their willingness to be reasonable, and the calendar was the thing that could have given you leverage. Days before end date Action 180 Pull utilization. Decide whether this is a renew, renegotiate, downsize, consolidate, or exit. If renegotiate or exit, name the alternative and start evaluating it, visibly. 120 Send the vendor a written notice of intent to renegotiate, with the specific asks. Ask for the price of the alternative in writing. Involve procurement. 90 Serve any contractual non-renewal notice required to preserve the option, even if you expect to renew. A served notice can be withdrawn; a missed one cannot. 60 Final terms agreed or the exit plan in motion. Anything still open here is being negotiated under time pressure, which is the vendor's preferred condition. 0 Signed terms filed in one place, calendar updated with the new dates, utilization baseline reset. The negotiation that matters most happens at the first signing, because that is when the renewal terms are set. These are the clauses to fix then, and to fix retroactively at the next renewal if they were missed. Clause Ask for Why Renewal uplift A cap (ideally zero to 3 percent, or tied to a published index), applying to every renewal rather than only the first An uncapped uplift is a blank cheque; a cap on the first renewal only moves the problem one year Auto-renewal and notice No auto-renewal, or a notice period of 30 days or less, and the vendor's obligation to notify you 90 days before the deadline Puts the burden of the calendar on the side that benefits from you missing it Seat flexibility The right to reduce seat count at renewal, and true-down at least annually for consumption Otherwise every optimistic forecast becomes a permanent floor Price hold and most-favored terms Pricing held for the full term, and a commitment that new customers of similar size are not offered materially better terms Prevents the list price from being renegotiated in the middle of a term through a product repackaging Tier and packaging protection Features you have today stay in your tier for the term; repackaging cannot force an upgrade Repackaging is the most common way SaaS vendors raise effective prices without touching the rate card Data exit Full export in a documented, non-proprietary format, at no charge, within 30 days of termination, with the data retained for that period Without this the switching cost is whatever the vendor decides it is. In the EU, the Data Act now supports switching rights for cloud services; use it Termination for convenience or for cause A clear right to terminate for material breach including SLA failure, and where possible for convenience with a notice period A contract that can only end at the renewal date has one negotiation point per term Security and compliance Right to audit or to receive current attestations, breach notification within a defined window, sub-processor change notice, and the ability to object See Regulatory Map for the regimes that make this mandatory rather than optional Assignment and change of control The contract survives your own change of control and the vendor's, at the same terms Otherwise an acquisition on either side reopens the price; see M&A Diligence Kit Service levels with teeth Credits that are meaningful, an escalation path, and termination rights after repeated failure A 99.9 percent SLA with a 5 percent credit is a marketing statement Vendors run renewals as a sales process with a playbook, a quota, and a quarter-end. Most customers run them as an admin task. The asymmetry is the whole problem. Know your number before theirsUtilization, value realized, the cost of the alternative including migration, and the internal budget. If you cannot say what the product is worth to you, the vendor will say it for you. Make the alternative credibleAn evaluation of a competitor, or of doing without, changes the vendor's behavior more than any argument. It works best when it is no bluff at all, and it has to be visible either way. Use the vendor's calendarVendors discount at their quarter-end and year-end. If your renewal date does not align, ask to move it. A three-month extension to reach their fiscal year-end is often worth more than any other single lever. Trade term for price, carefullyA longer commitment is the vendor's favorite ask. Accept it only with the uplift cap, the seat flexibility, and the exit terms above, so that a three-year deal does not become three years of leverage for them. Bundle the asksBring the clause corrections, the price, and any service issues to the same conversation. Vendors will fix contract terms in exchange for a renewal they were worried about; they will not reopen the contract mid-term. Escalate above the account executiveThe AE's discount authority is limited and their incentive is to close at the highest price that does not lose the deal. A conversation between your executive and theirs, at the right moment, changes both. Get everything in the order formVerbal commitments about roadmap, support, or future pricing are worth nothing at the next renewal. If it matters, it is in the signed document. The pattern recurs at every scale. The contract for a collaboration platform, $400k a year, 2,000 seats, auto-renews at 8 percent with 90 days' notice. Nobody notices until the invoice arrives at $432k. Utilization was 1,300 seats. The vendor points to the notice clause. The organization pays $432k for a year, of which roughly $150k is for seats nobody uses, and is now negotiating the following year from the same position. At 180 days, utilization shows 1,300 active seats. A competitor evaluation begins, visibly. At 120 days the vendor is told the intent is to renew at 1,400 seats, flat price per seat, with an uplift cap and true-down rights, or to migrate. At 90 days non-renewal notice is served to preserve the option. The vendor, facing a quarter-end and a live competitor, agrees to 1,400 seats at a 5 percent per-seat discount, 3 percent cap, annual true-down. The renewal lands at $266k. The difference funds two engineers. Handing renewals to procurement produces better paper and the same shelfware, because procurement can negotiate the rate but not the seat count, the tier, or whether the product is needed at all. Procurement negotiates a 7 percent discount on a renewal for a tool the engineering team stopped using six months ago. The discount is reported as a saving. The tool is renewed for two more years. Every contract has a business owner who answers three questions at 180 days: are we using it, do we still need it, and what is it worth. Procurement then negotiates the terms for the answer. Tie the owner's answer to the utilization data rather than their preference, and make the total contract value by owner visible in the technology budget so that shelfware has a name attached to it.
